Dear Madam--wnl you please tell me how
to pickle beets to keep all winterf should the
vinegar be boiled before pouring over the beets?
Also would like a recipe for ohow,chow >,

Picked beets-Chop one quart OF beets
fine, add one cupful grated horseradish, one
teaspoonfu salt and one-half teaspoonfui
paprika. Scald sufficient vinegar to cover
the whole mixture. reheat together to the
boiling point, place in sterilized jars and
seal.


Chow-chow-One large caulilower, one
dozen and a half small cucumbers one pint
pickling onions very smalD. six small green
peppers. two small red peppers, one quart
vinegar two tablespoonfuls mustard, one
tablespoonful turmeric one cupful salt Peel

water then drain. Separate the caullfower

half hour. Put the onions in a bowl, the

The transports and destroyers, all
though fairly confident that the U-boat
would scarcely dare show herself again,
even for pot-shot. were nevertheless
taking every precaution. Every ship
was at full speed. oil-burning destroy
ers constantly protecting their charges.
The whole attack occupied bare seconds.
Convoy and charges were out of range
in n few minutes at the most. Nowhere
had there been the slightest panic or
furry, but movements of men and ships
made with almost automatic precision
and speed. The efficiency of the British
naval man is the efficiency Of clock
work. Every cog knows it's place.
There Is no meddling, no clashing, no
Interference, but confident rapid eff
cheney which somehow demands the
use of the adjective deadly" Twenty
minutes later the transports were
safe in their port of destination
and the destroyer convoy was off again,
thirty miles an hour down the coast,
to it's next appointment.


Meanwhile, the business Of seeking
out the enemy was going on in the
fleet Of submarine hunters which had
gathered around blank buoy" Just
how the work was done and just what
was the result it is not permitted to
tell.

Sir: The inclosed poem was sung as the
Russian hymn at the recent war service at
the Church of st. John the Evangelist Since
Russia no longer has a Gar, the existing
Russian national hymn was inappropriate.
The Rev. John A. Wade, the rector, adapted to
suit the occasion Pope's hymn, Rise,
Crowned with Light, Imperial Salem, Rise!"
which, with these changes, seems TO make an
admirable Russian anthem:
Rise crowned with light, great Mother


Russia, rise


Exalt thy towering head and lift thine eyes
See heaven its sparkling portals wide display,
And break upon thee in food of day.
See strong race thy far-fung steppes adorn
See future sons, and daughters yet unborn,
In crowdng ranks on every side arise,
Demanding life, impatient for the skies.
See sister nations at thy gates attend.
Walk in thy light, and in thy temple bend!
See heaven born Liberty in bright array,
We, Freedoms sons, our joyous homage pay.
The seas shall waste, the skies to smoke


decay.


Rocks fall to dust, and mountains melt away;
But Russia, fixed. her mighty power remains;
Thy realms shall last, thy true Deliverer


reigns.


HERBERT p WILLIAMS.

An American destroyer has been severely
damaged in European waters in collision
with a British warshp, the Navy Depart.
ment announced today

part of the crew and towed the American
to port, where she has since been repaired
and sent back to active service.

accident, which was caused by the destroyer
suddenly coming out of a heavy ranstorm
that made her invisible. Accordingly an
investigation board eXonerated all con-
cerned from blame.


The destroyer had an immense hole in
her side, two davits carried away, the gal
ley and funnel broken and the foremast
smashed. Only the fact that the destroyer's s
watertight compartments were closed pre-
vented her sinking.


When the American vessel was towed in
her entire afterpart was awash. The Brit
ish ship with which she collided had her
stern badly twisted, but was not seriously
damaged.

Correspondence of the Associated Press.


LANDI KOTAL FORT, Khyber Pass.
Northwest Frontier. India, December
31.-A demonstration of the present
amicable relations between the British
government and Afghanistan was af-
forded a correspondent of the Asso-
ciated Press here in Khyber pass.
Claims and counterclaims regarding
the attitude of the Amir Of Afghanistan
toward the combatants in the world
war have been made continually since
the outbreak of hostilities. but this
much may be affirmed with certainty:


Great caravans, composed of thou
sands of camels and donkeys, heavily
laden with fruits and goods, are pour
ing into India from Afghanistan
through this gateway between the two
countries. Manifestly. these peaceable
pilgrimages could not be undertaken
were conditions other than quiet. More
over, and perhaps still more signifi-
cant, hundreds of Ghilzai, the nomads
of Afghanistan, are making their an
nual journey into the peninsula with
the caravans for trade and for the pur-
pose of securing places as laborers in
various sections. These coolies will
remain in India until spring, unofficial
hostages for the continued good rela-
tions between the amir and his power
full neighbor.


The formalities demanded by the neu-
trality of Afghanistan are being rigidly
adhered to by the British. From the
heights about this fort, which is ut
the top of the pass and only four miles
inside the international line. one can
see far out toward Kabul, but no one
not connected with the officially sane
toned caravans does more than look.
for to venture over the border wuld
give rise to the gravest consequences.
The amir is very Jealous of his rights
and is always suspicious Of foreigners
within his domains.

mishes with bands of raiding tribes
men the Khyber Rifles at Landi Kotal

the caravans which the amir permits

such caravans are under armed escort

tionally large. The correspondent saw

posed of fifteen hundred or more
camels and many donkeys. The trains
coming from Afghanistan will go back
ward and forward between Cabul and

oner demonstrates the rapidly OIL

Canadians generally, in the period be-
fore the United States declared war
Judged the American attitude little
harshly. They were critical of our slow
ness i'm resenting German aggression
They did not make allowances for the
strength of the influences here which were
condemning us to passivity. Genuine
Americans also deplored those influences,
but, having a closer view Of them, did not
underestimate them.


Now, when she is about to go on a con-
scription basis, Canada realizes to what
extent reluctance to go to war may mani
fest itself even among a relatively homo
geneous, un-hyphenated people. There
are two strains of blood in Canada's popu-
lation. But it is impossible to call either
element hyphenated in the American sense,
for the French Canadians have lived on
Dominion soil longer even than the Eng
disappearing Canadians have. Yet with
no conflicting blood or cultural ties (tor
France and Great Britain are now allies)
the French Canadians have shown sur
prising Discrimination either to enlist or to
support the war otherwise. They have
practised the pacifsm which our pacifists
have so far only talked about. Conscrip-
ton has been deferred for nearly three
wears because of the fear that it would
bring about clash between the English
sneaking and the French-speaking ele-
mentS.


Americans will sympathize with the
Canadian government in its dilemma. And
looking back at our exhibition of indecision
and our lack Of unified national feeling,
due to the pro-German and the pacifist
elements. both alien and native, in our
population. English-speaking Canadians
will doubtless now modify their former
critical attitude toward US. Our predica-
ment was for long time graver than
theirs. But we have extricated ourselves
They will extricate themselves also. Each
country will achieve through war far
greater unifcaton. And in doing so each
will become more sympathetic with the
other. Having worked and fought to-
gether and overcome similar anti-war dis
affection at home, the United States and
Canada will find themselves standing
closer together than ever before. They
will be more appreciative neighbors and
warmer friends.

nounced the repulse Of all Italian ef-
forts. Yet to-day's Austrian report de-

ment asserts, "all counter attacks have

plan.


This kept up, Mrs. Lyman said, until

claims against her, but those who had
profited most by her scheme tried 10
brighten her into leaving the country

she said.


Tried to Drown Her


The attempt on her life, she said,
was made when she was boarding a
launch at City Island with her bust
ness associates, intending to make a
trip TO Oyster Bay. Mrs. Hyman said

and she would have drowned but for
outside aid. She said she had more

way station of the Brighton Beach line
last Friday night.

ney Colnon, and grand jury investi-
cation will be started in a few days.

munity and be witness against her
accusers, whom she charges with con-
spiracy.

were arrested at the hearing before
Commissioner Gilchrist. They are:


Mr.. and Mrs. Grossman and the for
mer's father, Samuel Grossman; Mrs

her husband, George Leavy; Leonard

How long will France fight? What
is the morale of the French people


These are the questions asked Of me
the most frequently since my return
to this country. The answer lies with
the men who ask the questions. Every
American who asks how long France
will fight is himself the answer.


The Germans had famous slur on
the English at the beginning of the
war. It was a conversation alleged to
have taken place in Brussels between
the Kaiser and Belgian statesman.


"How long will Germany fght?' the
Belgian asked.


Germany will fight until she has
eaten her last dog and cat the Kaiser
replied.


"And how long will England ight?"
the Belgian inquired.


England will fight until the last
Frenchman is dead" said the Kaiser.


No one ever found it necessary to
ask how long France would fight.
Every one knew without asking that
France would fight until her last man
was dead. And so she will. What was
true of France at the beginning of the
war is just as true to-day-always pro-
viding that America does her part, and
does it promptly and effectively.


How long France will fight depends
entirely on America. For she cannot
continue the struggle without Ameri-
can help. The man power of France
has been used up to the extent that
she cannot keep up her reserves after
September. A soldier put out of &C
ton will then mean place left vacant
in the trenches.

behind the dunes are well garrisoned,
and an excellent system Of roads run
ming parallel with the coast enabled

tillery and infantry to any threatened
spot within less than an hour. Tor
pedo boats and a flotilla of submarines
patrol the coast at all times. Thus far
they have been able to save the lives
Of many shipwrecked sailors, but they
have not been called upon to do active
service.

town

breakfast.

stewards department and when il was
found breakfast had not been prepared a
search of the vessel was made The men
are said to have been with the ship for

New Britain is under martial law to
day, with two companies of State
guardsmen patrolling its streets, fol
lowing nine simultaneous fires in diff
ferent parts of the city last night.
Two men are under arrest on sus-
picion.


Repairs are being rushed on the
electric fire alarm system, which
broke down when several persons
turned in simultaneous alarms.


Local fire departments were still at
work early today quenching smolder-
ing embers. Volunteer engine compa-
MES from Hartford, Bristol, Water
bury, Plaintield have been sent home.


New Britain has many factories
which have been making munitions
for the entente allies. The belief was
expressed that some fanatic, hoping
to stop their manufacture, set the
fires by means of time incendiary
bombs, but no evidence OF bombs has
been found A tenement house, three
residences, a garage, a synagogue,
and a business block were destroyed
The damage is estimated at 5000.


Fire alarms came in rapid success
sion, and soon all apparatus was
working, and appeals for assistance
had been sent to nearby cities.


Companies 1 and L, First Infantry
were called out. and soon had re
stored order. BY midnight all blazes
were out and the city quiet.


The electric light, water, and gas
plants here have been placed under
military guard by Governor Holcomb

The soldier spirit is strong. Attach


ments formed among comrades in arms


are enduring Memories of hardships,
perils. victories and defeats abide. No
subsequent experiences. however graft
flying or thrilling, dim those of war and
| war times.


We saw this at the meeting of the
Confederate veterans III this town in
June. assembled in comradeship and
good feeling They were old men, more


than half century distant from the
struggle in which they had staked ALL
and lost. But they delighted in one an
| Others company. They wore their uni
forms with pride quite youthful-that
defed the years. They marched with
relish The old time came over them
and made them young again for the oc-
casion.


We are about to witness the same
thing in Boston, where. in a few days,
the Grand Army of the Republic will
hold its ffty-frst annual encampment


The survivors Of the host that saved the


Union are old men. But they, too, de-
light in one another's company, and
wear their uniforms with pride that
defes time. The distance from the days
of their exploits does not affect them in
their desire TO show their continuing
love of country.


This appears in their decision TO hold
the usual parade. The suggestion that
they are now too old for such demon
stration was rejected. They will march,
and IN larger numbers than recently.
The occasion, as they think, calls for an
unusual display by them They hope
it will contribute toward rousing
stronger martial spirit in the country.
The men who have been called to the
colors and are on the eve of going into
camp to prepare for going into battle
may see in the spirit of these veterans
something that awaits them They, too.
while in uniform will contract attach
ments lasting while they live. The
camp, the march, the battle will draw
them close to one another, and give them
experiences that will never fade out of
their hearts or minds. Fifty years
hence those fortunate enough to reach
that time will probably meet, as these
veterans of the civil war now are meet
ing, to recall old days and renew their
devotion to the country and its insti
buttons.


War is hell, but not unmitigated hell.
Great things grow out of it; and the
forces that rule the world are sometimes
recast in wars furnace into better and
more serviceable shapes.

ITALIAN ARMY HEADQUARTERS
IN NORTHERN ITALY, Friday, Nov
3O.-A colonel commanding batteries
along the Asiago front, where the Aus
TRANS and Germans are exerting their
chief pressure, took the correspondent
along his lines to-day and explained
the situation and the action in prog
ress.


From his observation post at the
summit of the mountains thanking the
Asiago plateau one could look down
on the shell-torn and deserted city Of
Asiago, now held by the enemy, with
his lines of intrenchments beyond and
his batteries blazing from the long
range Of SUBMITS extending from
Monte Meletta eastward to the Brenta
River.


Ii was a most impressive mountain
scene, at an altitude of 5000 feet, with
the clouds lying below instead OF
above, and the cannonade echoing
through the gorges. The ground was
covered with an inch OF snow, when
had fallen in the night. and the ponds
formed in shell holes were coated with
three inches of ice.


The men off duty we're around camp
fires, looking well and contented. The
colonel said living conditions, rations
and supplies were in good shape.


Some of the men were IN tents on
the mountain slopes, some in trenches
and dugouts, while others were in
rough frame barracks which were being
hastily constructed.


Asiago its>r presented a desolate
spectacle in the midst Of the fire-swept
plateau, TO which 1t gives its name,
with the Italian on one side and the
enemy on the other Houses, churches
and tall Companies could be seen
plainly, but the colonel said the whole
place was in ruins, without a building
intact. Strong field glasses showed no
sign OF life in the town, and no smoke
arose from the factories or residences.


The artillery was heavy and con-
tinuous. The colonel said the enemy
was bringing up heavy guns OF large
caibre. Twenty monster projectiles
had come in a bunch early in the day,
opening great craters, which were now
frozen ponds. There had been no in
fantry advances, and the colonel was
satisfied with the repulse the enemy
had received. The enemy would doubt
less attempt another advance. the col
onel said. but the strength of the
Italian lines gave assurance that he
would be repulsed again.


Austrian prisoners who had been
brought in declared that they recently
came from the Russian front. The
enemy lines were made up, according
10 this officer, of Germans and Aus
TRANS, but there were no Bulgarisns
or Turks. The wild nature of this
country was shown while the soldiers
were digging their trenches. when they
unearthed the fossil remains of num-
erous mastodons Of gigantic dimen-
sions.


Along the road leading to the front
there was increasing activity, with vast
forces OF men and material pushed for
ward The correspondent passed bat
teries of heavy guns drawn BY trains.
tractors and huge stacks Of 8 and r.
irch shells. Infantry was moving for
ward, being strung along the road for
three miles. This and frequent evil
dences Of troops on many roads gave
visible sign Of the power being con-
centrated, while on every hand the Off
GERS and men were confident that the
enemy's great drive from the north had
been held as that from the Piave side

soldiers killed and at least half that num-

acted by Mexican bandits who attacked
a National Line train near San Felipe, in
the state of Hidalgo. Monday night
The survivors who reached here tonight
declare that the bandits lost at least
twenty killed and about an equal number
wounded.


The coaches of the train bear unmis-
taxable evidence of the viciousness Of the
battle. The woodwork is perforated with
bullet holes and all the windows arc
shattered.


The scene of the attack was between
San Luis Potosi and Queretaro. a desolate G
stretch of country The bandits shot the
engineer. mounted the cab, and brought
the train to a stop. They then fired
a volley into the coaches. The Car
rama soldiers returned the fire. and the
battle did not cease until every govern
ment trooper was shot. The bandits then
allowed the train to proceed toward
Nueve Laredo. The alarm was given at
San Luis Potosi and troops started in
pursuit Of the bandit band, said to num-
ber about 800 men.

let to-day by the Emergency Fleet Cor
poration to the American international
Corporation.

signed for the three new plants In which
the Government will have built a large
number Of fabricated ships. The Hog
Island plant will cost slightly less than
$4,000. 900. The other contracts will
20 to the Submarine Boat Corporation
for a plant at Newark and to the Mer-
chants Shipbuilding Company for one at
Chester. Pa.


The first OF the fifty ships will be
completed by the American International
Corporation within Ten or eleven months
and the entire number will be finished
probably within fifteen or sixteen
months. Long before they are finished,
lihood will have asked for additional
money to build more ships.


Shipping Board officials believe that
the fabrication of ships will mean that
America within few years will have
the largest fleet Of merchant ships of
any nation In the world.


The fabricating programme calls for
manufacture of the parts for the ships
In the steel mills and only the assembly
Of their pacts in the yards. Some off,
cials believe that fabricating methods

Petrograd, Friday, July 27.-When
the Russian women's battalion, known
officially as the Command OF Death"
went into action against the Germans
near Smorgon, July %, it captured sew
eral women, from whom it was learned
for the first time that German women
also were fighting on the battle front
in Western Russia. Ten wounded hero
ines of the women's battalion arrived
in Petrograd to-day, leaving their COM
mander, Vera Butchkaref, and Marya
Skrydloff, a daughter of Admiral
Skrydloff, former commander OF the
Baltic fleet and Minister of Marine, IN
hospital at Vitebsk.


Interviewed, the women said it was
reported that of the 200 of the COM
mand who reached the front only fifty
remained. Twenty were killed, eight
were taken prisoner and all the rest
were wounded.


Several times" said one wounded
girl, I'VE attacked the Germans. Espe-
cially memorable was our attack at
Novospassky Wood, near Smorgon,
where the enemy, hearing the voices
of girls. lost their nerve. The result
was that many of them were killed,
wounded or taken prisoner Among
the prisoners were few women, from
whom we learned for the first time
that German women also were fighting


1--WE did not feel the slightest fear
for our personal safety. Our passion
was to serve the fatherland. We ad-
vanced gayly against the foe with
laughter and song, our only unpleas-
ant sentiments being when we first
came to the corpses. Once, when re-
plying to the enemy's severe rifle and
machine gun fire, we discovered to our
amazement that all our men COM
rades in the neighboring trenches had
treacherously fed. leaving us-a hand
full of women-to face the enemy
alone"

south Atlantic sea raiders as the

lished with the arrival here today OF
eleven sailors, seven of whom are
Americans, who were members of the
crew of the British steamship st. Theo-
dore.

ish freighter early in January, turned
the St Theodore into raiding vessel
by mounting guns on her deck and
supplying her with German crew

of destroying entente vessels, and the
men arriving here today said they were
allowed to witness, from the cruisers
deck, the sinking of two French sailing
vessels and five British steamships.

New York, April s.--A mother and her
little baby boy lay dead tonight in a
Brooklyn police station-the little child a
victim of the woman's insane act

the smiling, white-dressed mite OF hu-
manity, started to walk across the Will
iamsburg Bridge Near the Brooklyn
tower she asked two young girls to hold
the baby for a few minutes She went
into the retiring room in the tower. The
baby, munching a cracker. cooed and
smiled at the young miss who was hold
ing him. Finally the mother appeared.
She was small OF stature. had dark eyes
and was neatly dressed In a brown sut.


She took the baby from the girl Then,
leaning over the inner rail, she dropped
her purse. perhaps purposely. With the
baby in her arms she climbed over the
rail. ostensibly to pick up her pocket
book. And then. before a hand could
stay her, she flung the baby over the
rail The little one had its life crushed
out on the Belgian block pavement, 100
feet below, almost at the foot of two OF
the special police guards stationed there
to watch the bridge.


And before the officers, unnerved by
the shock, could gather their senses, a
shadow fell across them from above. A
moment later the woman's body crashed
head FIRST upon the pavement She had
followed her murderous act by jumping
to death.

were still unidentified. -..-.- ..

American soldiers who go to France

the first time to-day. and further that

maintains that the conditions here have

me mub became unmanageable and

Eight hundred and fifty men of the
United States Army ambulance serv-
ice dined al fresco on the Ellipse this
afternoon. while several hundred Wash
ingtonians stood around and watched
a demonstration of how the government
feeds its soldiers in the field. The
meal was prepared in seven field kitch-
ems, from raw materials carried in the
huge Army trucks.


The demonstration was intended to
show just how meals are prepared and
served to men close behind the fighting
lines. where there is no chance for them
to go to mess halls. The entire corps
here from the camp at Allentown. Pa.
ate the dinner, which consisted of hot
pork and beans corned beef. bread and
coffee. All but the bread was cooked
in the field kitchens, which ale drawn
behind the supply trucks.


Parade Precedes Dinner.


Preceding the demonstration dinner
the corps paraded past the White
HOUSE and the State. War and Navy
building, where it was reviewed by
President Wilson and surgeon General
Gorgas.


The big trucks and field kitchens
were then drawn up around the Ell
lipse and the Army cooks began pre-
pairing the meal. fires already having
been started in the kitchens. Box after
box Of pork and beans was opened and
hundreds OF cans of the Army staple
were placed in the big mess pans and
shot into the ovens to heat. Coffee was
put over the fire in the big boilers;
corned beef was sliced and made ready.
and in surprisingly short time the
meal was ready and mess call sounded.


Show Housekeeping" Ability.


After dinner the men showed how
the mess kits are washed and put away
for the next meal. while scores of
mothers, sisters and others of the city's
feminine population gathered around
and praised or criticized the housekeep-
ing ability displayed by the ambulance
men.


When the after-dinner work was out
of the way. the corps fell in. and. pre-
ceded by the band. marched to Pennsyl-
vania avenue and back to Fort Myer.
where the men are quartered until they
return to Allentown tomorrow evening
or Friday,

Derby minister of war, addressing the
Canadian Club dinner at Folk estone
last night, said that the allies had made
great mistakes during the war, but
their enemies had made far greater
mistakes and were gradually arriving
at the conclusion that they had been
using the wrong map. He feared that
there was a likelihood of much more
fighting and much more sorrow and
misery for the nation before the war
would end.

that the enemy was demoralized. That
was not true The enemy is still fight
ing, and is not demora1ized. Although
the Germans are fighting well the al
lies are fighting far better. Comment
ing on the replies Of the central en-
pires to the Pope. Lord Derby said the
day had gone by when any king or
government could make war The
only authority able to make war or
bring it about was the people them
selves, and the only thing the allies
could do now. bearing in mind what
Germany had dome to civilization, was
to fight on.

London. Jan. 28.-The Teutonic

Rumania began. On both the East

lie Transloy marked the night and

Russians.

sian Farman plane and German battle

North Of Verdun the French ad-
vanced last night and penetrated the
enemy's trenches between the Calonne
trench and Les Eparges, on the right

Paris states.

Prince maintained their positions.


British patrols and raiding parties
were extremely active last night and
this morning. The German trenches
we're entered northeast of Neuville-St-

citrate the British lines near Fauquis-
sart broke down before the intense fire

London, July 11.-To-day's Admiralty
report on shipping losses for last week
shows that, with one exception, enemy
U-boats had less success against Brit
ish vessels than in any week since the
ruthless" submarine campaign was in
augurated. Among British merchant
men of more than 1900 tons, only
fourteen were sunk, while three small
cr craft and seven fishing vessels were
also sent down.


The lowest figure previously record
cd was that for the week ended March
10. when thirteen large British ships
and four smaller ones were destroyed.
The most disastrous week was that
ended on April 2l, when forty capital
ships and fifteen smaller ones were
sunk.


For a month the submarine "wave"
has been ebbing, and apparently the
comparative ineffectivcness of last
weeks work represented the bottom of
the curve. which presumably will start
upward this week toward a new crest,
as another feet of the submersibles,
newly outfitted, issues from the Ger
man bases. Nevertheless, naval au
thorities here are gratified at the fig
urcs issued to-day, and point to a
dwindling average in U-boat destruc-
tiveness observed since the BLACK
week. last April.


Proves Patrols Effectiveness

is attributed largely to the increasing
effectiveness of the joint British and
American warship patrol. But it is
also admitted that as the submarines
expend their torpedoes they gradually
withdraw to home ports to wait until
the next feet is ready for operations.
There is no means of knowing how
many, if any, of the enemy underwater
craft were destroyed during the week,
but the published figures indicate that
they have had hard going recently.

ures OF ships of all nationalities, $500,

thin slices. but do not remove skin.

pressing through a sieve. Add the
seedlcss pulp and cook until the skins

Raisine.-Take an equal quantity of
grapes and pears. Wash and stem the
grapes. add just sufficient water to
keep from burning and let them sim
mer until soft. Then put them through
a sieve. Pare and core the pears and
cut in thin slices. Add the sliced pears
to the grape juice and let cook slowly
until the pears are tender. Stir fire.
quently to keep from burning. Weigh.
and to each cup of the pear and grape
mixture allow three quarters of a cup
of sugar. Cook until the consistency of
marmalade. Turn into glasses and seal.

don, Nov. PA report received from
the Western front describing the
American troops in action says:


Independent American units have
been thrown into the trench line. The
felt hat has given way to the English.
fashioned steel helmet, and the whist.
ling and bursting Of the shells have be-
come familiar sounds to American ears


"For the first time since they have
been participating as independent con

real earnestness of war, even though
it was but minor hand-to-hand scuf-
fe. But this time the shells did not
merely fly over their heads, but into the
very trenches they had selected, and
presently, with an internal noise, these
things which the young soldiers be-

quake and burst.


And hard on the heels of this a
firm attack by our onrushing Bavarian
reserves forced the way into the Amer
lean trenches, and musket shots and
bursting hand grenades relieved the
artillery fire.

termined defence, and desperate hand
to-hand fighting set in. Butts of guns,
fists and hand grenades were freely
brought into play. and many men fell
to the ground before the rest gave up
resistance and surrendered. After a
bare hour the German storming troops
were back in their own trenches with
booty and prisoners.

young men from the land of liberty
They were sturdy and sportsmanlike in
build. Good natured smiles radiated
from their blue eyes, and they were
quite surprised that we did not pro-
pose TO shoot them down. as they had
been led in the French training camp
to believe we would do.

American Training Camp in France,

Pershing, commander Of the American

camp to-day, tomorrow and Wednes-
day was withheld from the American
troops until this morning, in order
that the general might see the actual
everyday working conditions-that he
might find the men at their daily task
without undue preparations being
made for his inspection.


General Pershing, motoring from
Paris, is expected to arrive at the field
headquarters late this afternoon, when
he will be received with honors beft-
ting his rank as commit nder in chief
of the expeditionary forces.


The inhabitants Of the French viii
lage where the American headquarters
are located quickly sensed to-day the
fact that something important was
about to happen, and there was much
enthusiasm when they heard who was
coming. The simple peasant folk
brought out their French flags, and the
tiny village assumed quite an air of
gayety. There was much speculation
as to how to pronounce General PERISH
ing's name, the nearest approach TO 1t
being "Peer-shan," with that distinct
French nasal sound on the last sylla-
bic.

splendid condition physically and the
equipment in the best of order. Some
scattered units Of the American force
have been having great difficulty with
their mail, which seems to have gone
astray. Tkis is particularly true of
the Red Cross hospital units which re-
Gently arrived and is causing much
concern among the doctors, nurses and
enlisted men, who fear their folks at
home will think something untoward
has happened to them. II can be stated
that all the members of the Roosevelt
and Johns Hopkins units are we'll and
happy and anxious for their real work
to begin.


One difficulty about the mail has
been that letters destined for Ameri-
can units in charge of British base
hospitals have come to the hospital
units here, and it is presumed that
some mails which should have come
here have been misdirected there.

While thousands OF bursting shells
were wiping out great factory and
threatening to destroy a Jersey town,
not more than ten miles away, New
York City went plscidly about its ousl-
ness yesterday afternoon and gave no
thought to what was occurring on the
other side of the Hudson.


Not until the late editions Of the
afternoon papers bore news Of the ex-
plosion did most of the jewellers IN
Manhattan know it had occurred. A few
heard the distant rumble that contin-
ued from o'clock until long after dark,
and a handful in high Office buildings
saw the great cloud of smoke that
piled up out OF Jersey and streamed
away to the south, clear across the
windows. But these only said idly that
there must be nre somewhere, and
turned again TO their work.


Riverside Drive, where the best view
OF the great smoke was afforded, was
practically deserted all the afternoon.
A few paused to look at the mighty
billowing cloud and listen to the far
away rumble, but the north wind was
too strong for them, and they soon
fed.


After dark those who dwell in apart
ment houses along the drive watched
the crimson glow far down on the SKY
line. Those who used field glasses in
sisted that they were able 10 see the
twinkle Of shells bursting against the
black sky.


According TO the police reports from
The Bronx, the blast was felt more
heavily there than in Manhattan. On
Citv Island and the Kingsbridge dis
trict houses were shaken and WINDOWS
smashed


AS far north as Mount Vernon and
New Rochelle the explosions were felt.
Dwellers in these towns called Fort
Slocum on the telephone, believing that
the big guns were in action there.


The force of the explosion was felt
at Hastings, which is on the east bank
of the Hudson, twenty-one miles from
the Grand Central Station. The fire.
lit sky could also be seen from the top
Of the hill there.


So severely were Westchester and
Rockland counties Jared by the mu-
nitions explosion that Sing Sing
PRISONS old structures were shaken.
Glass In the outbuildings on Mrs.
Thomas Fortune Ryan's country place
in Suffern was broken.


The rumblings could be heard. the
shock felt and the flashes seen by
the convicts in the prison.


Yonkers felt the explosion for two
hours and the police and fire depart
ments' telephones we're kept busy by
anxious persons.

The trees are in their autumn beauty,
The woodland paths are dry,
Under the October twilight the water
Mirrors a still sky,
Upon the brimming water among the stones
Are nine and fifty swans.
The nineteenth autumn has come upon me
Since first made my count
! saw, before had we'll finished,
All suddenly mount
And scatter wheeling in great broken rings
Upon their clamorous wings.
But now they drift on the still water
Mysterious, beautiful;
Among what rushes will they build,
By what lakes edge or pool
Delight mems eyes when ! awake some day
To find they have flown away?
I have looked upon these brilliant creatures
And now my heart is sore.
Al's changed since !, hearing at twilight
The first time on this shore
The bell-beat of their wings above my head,
Trod with lighter tread.
Unwearied STILL lover by lover,
They paddle in the cold
Companionabe streams or climb the air;
Their hearts have not grown old,
Passion or conquest, wander where they will,
Attend upon them still.


WILLIAM BUTLER YEATS.

With temperatures ranging from two to
eight below zero in all sections of the
state, Ohio today experienced the cold
est December weather since 1880, when
the mercury dropped to II degrees be-
low zero.

at Springfield were reported, due to
the excessive cold. The coal shortage
was acute in most cities of the state.

any coal at all, due to the car short
age. Great suffering was reported
among the tenement districts of the
cities.


Railroad, traction, telegraph and tele-
phone service was demoralized, trains
running hours late.


The Scioto valley traction line, be-
tween Columbus and Chillicothe. sus-
pended operations altogether both yes
terday and today, causing many Camp
Sherman soldiers, home on furloughs.
to overstay their leaves.


Dayton and Cincinnati were the cold

below zero. Toledo and Cleveland reg
istered 2 below and Columbus below.

wind.

points reported without fuel

Paris, July 22.-Game hunting will
be allowed this year for the first time
since 1913. The season will open only
after the crop has been harvested and
will be short. The government has de-
cided that this measure is necessary to
protect agriculture against the raw
ages of the game, which has multiplied
greatly in the three years during
which only restricted destruction Of
depredating animals has been allowed.


Hares, rabbits, pheasants and par
tridges are particularly abundant, while
wild boar, driven from the forests OF
northeast France by the military op-
erations, have done considerable dam
age in regions where they were never
seen before. The opening of the hunt
ing season, besides saving the crops,
is expected to help relieve the pro-
visions market. while the issue of hunt
ing licenses will aid the state treasury.

mitted TO hunt without license, while

brilliant audience composed OF
members of Congress, the diplomatic
corps, and distinguished guests.

admirals, and diplomatic agents of

ton.

airplane evolutions above the clouds,

greeted the initial picture which
showed Marshal Joffre and Gen.
Pershing exchanging greetings and
French leaders in action, among them

leve.

German aerial scouting airplane

air battle. Pitching headlong down
wards like a wounded bird, the Teu-

PLATTSBURG. Aug. 25.-The entire
student body Of the second officers
training camp, three thousand strong,
slept tonight in the unpainted bar
racks which will be their homes for the
next three months.


All this morning the second incre-
ment poured into camp. and practically
the entire roster had been filled and
each Of its members equipped, in so far
as the authorities were able to outfit
them, by early afternoon.


The men who have come here TO be
hammered and tempered into efficient
fighting machines are oil from the New
, England states and New York. Until
Monday morning they will be con-
cerned chiefly with getting their bear
ings and preparing their equipment for
the three gruelling months ahead.


So far the discipline has been light
and the work of an extremely mild
character. At $3.50 Monday morning
the work will change entirely for the
candidates. From then on they will
be run through one of the hardest
courses of training ever devised by
men, anu Oo uhhOic
10 stand up beneath the work which
will be piled upon them. But those
who emerge with the coveted strips
Of brown braid about their blouse
sleeves will be men that the nation
may trust.


Already many OF tho candidates who
nave had no previous military expert
ence arc working hard in the attempt
to gain some rudimentsry knowledge
before the real work sets in.


Groups of men gather about the pa
rade grounds and stumble through the
manual of arms under the direction Of
some more experienced company mate.
Others squat in a semi-circle and try 70
guess the words one OF their fellowG
spells out with the red semsphore
flags. Still others spend much time in
their barracks poring over books Of
military lore.


Tomorrow the work Of inoculating
all the newcomers against typhoid and
smallpox will begin. Those who have
returned from the first camp will not
be forced to go through this ordeal.
The men to-day were ordered 10 re-
main in camp until dates for the in
oculations were given out. Because of
this the usual Saturday half holiday
and Sunday off will be omitted this
week

Fall River, Mass. Jan. 2l.-There
was very little doing in the print clotn
markets last week The sales were rela-
,ively small and the demand far below
normal. Buyers proved that they were
not interested in market conditions and
there were few in the market last week
with any real intention of buying.


The wider styles we're in demand, but
even these did not have the attention
from buyers which they ordinarily
would have had were conditions even
normal in the cotton goods markets
The narrow end of the market was
ouiet and the volume of business done
was of small proportions.


Prices have gone off little and buy
ers have been able to obtain goods at
lower prices than those prevailing In
the open market. On some lines OF VIDE
STYLES the market Is bare, and any
goods which may be secured can COM
mand full asking prices. The transac-
tions among second hands are growing
smaller and prices which have been
named by these factors are having very
little effect on market quotations.
The call for sateens, wills and spe-
cialties was light and the business put
through was only nominal.
Conditions in the cotton yarn mar
kets were rather quiet last week. Prices
have gone off on some counts, while
others have suffered from the lack Of
a substantial demand. There are some
warns which cannot be purchased now,
even at premium prices, because spin
ners have all they can do to get do
liveries out on time.


Manufacturers of automobile fabrics
have bought very heavily Of desirable
counts, and these yarns cannot be pur-
chased in any quantity In the open
markets.


One of the features Of the week was
tho settlement of the strikes at the
Fall River Iron Works mills and the
Fall River Bleachery. These disturb
ances have been enduring for several
weeks.


The total sales OF cloth for the week
are estimated at $4,000 pieces, OF which
about Is, 1000 pieces are spots. The week
closed with the demand light and prices
not so steady.

man raiders, finding everybody ready

attack on the trenches.

tribute tracts, and scientists take
useful facts: we all take books

circumstances warranted.

young men whose enlistment as ambu-

expired had refused 10 enlist in the
American army and were lettering

lis; or return 20 America. The French
authorities will be asked TO cancel their

army authorities will take up their
passports unless they enlist or return

WITH THE BRITISH ARMIES IN

Arrangements were being com

The Americans are widely scatter

British fighting men, like the

Know What They Want.


Oranges, candy, cigarettes, razors,

prepared.


Incidentally a canvass OF the Tom
mics by their commanding officers to
find out just what sort Of things they
wanted for this Christmas spread has
developed some freakish appetites.


Pork and Beans Lead.


One captain asked his men whether
they wanted turkey or pork and beans
the latter piping hot, with strips of
bacon Drowned on the top. The pork
and beans won hands down in the sub
sequent vote.


British front. That much is certain.

It must have been the voice of Love


That this strange longing stirred:
For when 1 found the sea one day

The cities with their mighty throngs

Where all the pillows of the world

This process has been continued by
the British steadily since the recent
big offensive. The artillery has kept
up an almost unceasing thunder along
the whole front, and air raids and
thrusts by the infantry have been
working great destruction in the en-
emy territory.


Last nights infantry raids are ex-
amples OF the work being done, much of
which is never published to the outside
world. English and Scottish regiments
about midnight conducted three sue
cessful raids. East of Gavrelle several
prisoners were taken and a large num-
Der of the enemy killed. five big dug
outs were bombed to pieces and two
saps destroyed. A similar success was
achieved south of Arras, several dug
outs being demolished and a number of
trench mortar emplacements wrecked.
besides other damage done.


The British air service still maintains
supremacy and the big raiding ma
chimes have been doing vast damage.
One of the spectacular air incidents oc-
Cured yesterday. when British plane

ate. They are the income. excess profits

putting, levying and collecting Yet
these differences of opinion will not de-
lay the final enactment of the bill, for
the House conferees all believe the bill

confidence in that respect means that
the differences will be Smoothed away
and that the Senate bill will be the
measure to be enacted, with perhaps
few notifications.

London, June 13.--Ninety-seven per-
sons were killed and 437 maimed-al-
most half of them women and chill
dren-by a flock OF German aeroplanes
which swept over London just before
noon to-day in the deadliest air raid
of history.


Fifty-five men met death and 223
were wounded; sixteen women and
twenty-six children were killed, and
l22 women and ninetyfour children
were wounded.


The first bombs seemed to come from
nowhere. Then, like bright little
specks of metal, the enemy machines
could be made out shimmering in the
summer haze and darting in a wide
circle over the city, fully four miles
above the earth. The whole murderous
visit lasted only fifteen minutes, and
did no naval or military damage what
ever. In that time, however, the path
Of the invaders was marked by wide
swaths Of destruction, both in the
downtown section and through the
densely populated East End.

The bombing Of a school furnished
one of the most pitiable scenes in
the whole raid. The bomb struck the
roof squarely, cutting clean through
and passing through two classrooms,
one above the other, killing some
children, but sparing the majority. II
finally exploded with terrific force in
a room on the ground floor, where
there were sixty-four little children,
from FIVE to seven years old, ten OF
whom were killed outright. and all
the others were more or less injured.


The room was thirty-six feet by
twenty-four and the force of the ex-
plosion in such a confined area was
naturally terrific. A basin shaped hole
several feet deep was made in the
floor. Most Of the ceiling was brought
down and the furniture shattered into
splinters. Some of the babies had arms
and legs torn off, others were shock
ingly lacerated, some stunned and
others buried in the wreckage.


The room was filed with the screams
and means of the tiny sufferers, many
Of whom were crying distractedly for
their mothers. Helpers who rushed in
from the outside found four women
teachers wonderfully self-possessed,
although covered with blood, giving
what help was possible to their little
charges and trying 70 calm those who
we're only slightly hurt. Many Of the
children were lying limp and helpless
across the shattered desks, bleeding
from terrible wounds. Others were
writhing in pain, and some bodies were
unrecognizable.


The behavior of the London crowds
during the bombardment was remark
able. Many rushed for the refuge OF
the cellars, but as many more fought
excitedly for the privilege OF watch
ing the passage of the deadly birdmen.
Thousands Of Londoners, peering up
into the hazy sky, never saw the Ger
man fiers az all.


But they heard the home guns, which
ratified away almost with the eject
Of drumfre. The reports followed
one another almost every second,
shaking windows throughout the
city and almost drowning the de-
tonation Of the exploding bombs. Never
in previous raids have the guns been
brought so promptly or so accurately
into play, but the targets were prac-
tically invisible.


The greatest death and devastation
were spread through London's East
End, where hundreds OF small shops
were blown TO pieces. Whole blocks
Of streets here were shambles, but
the work Of rescue among the ruins
was quickly taken up. East Enders are
used 10 misery, but the scenes Of acute
suffering to-day were pitiable, especial
ly among the mothers of mangled chill
dren.

freaks, sometimes burying themselves
harmlessly, and again shattering every

A FRENCH PORT, Nov. 25.-Suffer-

three American naval airmen were
picked up by. a French patrol boat last
night, after having been lost at sea
for nearly sixty hours


The three men. in a huge triplsue
hydro o-airplane, left a French base
Thursday morning, IN search of four
enemy submarines. which were re-
ported operating of the coast.


When the men failed to return other
machines were sent out to search for
them. The searching machines, how
ever, returned after several hours and
reported that they had seen no trace
Of the missing plane or its crew.


The naval authorities then sent out
a general warning to all Allied boats
off the coast, and the search for the
Americans was continued throughout
Thursday night. all day and all night
Friday and throughout Saturday. with
naval air machines assisting in the
daylight hours.


About dusk Saturday French patrol
boat saw the missing machine drifting
helplessly several miles out at sea. A
boats crew rescued the three men. who
included Ensign Kenneth Smith,
former Yale student, who was the
pilot; Frank j. Brady, of Newark. n.
J.. observer and gunner, and !. +. Will
kenson. mechanician.


The three men were virtually ex-
hausted when picked up. They were
given first aid treatment on the boat,
which rushed them to this port, where
the men we're transferred to a relief
hospital All the men have now re-
covered.

ROME, September 29.-An Italian off,
Ger, until recently a war prisoner at
Lauthausen, Austria, now exchanged
owing to i'll health, gave The Star a
special interview. in which he said:


Austria knows she cannot win the
war. The emperor today would give the
entire Trentino to Italy for immediate
peace. but fears to give US Trieste and
also fears the kaiser.


Germany now quite dominates the
internal administration. The civil rural
population suffers terribly. but is well
disciplined. Vienna still enjoys racing
and social attractions. while all the
newly rich spend wildly.


Civil concentration camps are ter
rible. Both sexes are herded together
and almost naked. Well bred women
ing five miles, and bribing our sentries
to beg a little food from us. knowing
we got packages from home.


THE SerbianS and Russians are the
worst off of all. They will all suffer ter
ribly this coming winter, because the
prison authorities have announced that
no fuel is available. even II prisoners
are able to pay for it. Last winter we
managed to buy a small quantity of coal
dust. which gave out by January. Then.
despite the intense frost, we had no
fuel, but burned table legs and chairs
and our trestles

During the week of June the fourth
thirty thousand Confederate SOLDIER
will march in triumph through thu
streets of washington-from the Cap
itol to the White House.


And along the entire length of Penn
syIvania avenue it will be THE South
In the Saddle, and riding gloriously.


Fifty-six years ago this confident
announcement would have created
national panic. Today 1t is a welcome
proclamation of patriotism and peace.


Camped at last in their country's
Capital and lighting their bivouac
hres between the Washington Monu-
ment and the portico Of the Presi-
dents home, these battered and de-
crepit veterans of lost cause-sol-
diers of Jackson and johnson and Lee
will have conquered at last the hearts
of Washington, and achieved In peace
what they failed to accomplish at the
point of their bayonets in war.


First Meeting Here.


Never before have the Confederate
Veterans held a reunion In their coun-
try's capital. They have met for 81
years in every southern city. holding
their last reunion but one in Rich
mond-the capital of the Old Confed-
eracy-amid the glad hands and the
reminiscent tears Of that great OLD
Virginia breed that made them well
come there.


They cross the Potomac in June
for the first time-the 9th Reunion
of the United Confederate Veterans,
and the s2nd Reunion of the Sons OF
yeteran-and come to hold their
greatest and perhaps their last assem-
bIy-in washington-the Capital OF
their country now and forever.


The Grand Army Of the Republic has
held its reunion in Washington time after
time. With flags flying and brass bands
blaring and cannon booming, they have
swept the historic Avenue with fervent
and tender cheers. But the ''Tatterde-
MELONS Of Lee'-now good American citi-
zens-who for years looked grimly from
the Virginia hills upon the stately dome
of our House upon the hill, have never
before linked these faded Stars and Bars
in loving fellowship with the Star

ers and several clerks and customs in

wanna and Central Railroad of New

cannon-like explosions came nearer
As they stood watching there was a
sudden tremendous roar beneath their
feet. The men were thrown to the
ground and thus escaped the fame:

If any "idiotic Yankee" does not yet ap-
preciate the sincerity of German concern
for the little nations, there is new illu-
mination for him in the announcement
from Amsterdam that Belgium has been
divided into two districts. These two dis
tricts roughly follow the division between
the Flemings and the Walloons-that is,
between the people of Teutonic and of
French stock.


Without regard to the derivation Of the
Belgians. German armies have destroyed
Louvan, which was Flemish, and Dinant,
which was French. In the murder OF
children, the dishonor of women and the
assassination of men both races stood
equal in the German eyes. Even-handed
Boche Justice distributed atrocities 10 both
races, and the methodical Germans stole
the clocks, pillaged the banks, destroyed
the furniture with that thoroughness
which will remain memory throughout
the world for a century to come.


All of this, however, is nothing but a
logical and natural manifestation of Ger
man necessity, which should neither sur
prise nor excite the world. What is of
importance for humanitarians all over the
globe to know is that the Germans have
resolved to liberate the Flemish popula-
ton from all association with the French;
to create two Belgiums in the hope that
one of them may conceive affection for
the German and hatred for the French.


We shall now have stirring pronounce
ments from Berlin of the German solicit
tude for another little people, descriptions
Of the fashion in which the Germans are
"rescuing" the Flemings, like the Poles,
the Lithuanians and equally unfortunate
peoples. Americans reading these pro
nouncements should remember that Ger
man interest in the Flemings began with
the destruction of Louvain and AerschOt,
and was continued through the lombard
ment of Antwerp up to the dispatch of
chain gangs of Flemish workmen driven
to German trenches. If any Flemings
survive the German war of liberation it
NAV be questioned whether they will hate
their liberators less than the rest of civil
lied Europe does.

BY August, 1913, much progress had
been accomplished. Aeroplanes were then
used seriously by all the ARMIES for re-
connoissance and artillery observation.
Night flying had been developed. There
were many bombing raids, both by night
and day, and whereas in the year previous
the aeroplanes only weapon was the
pilots revolver, now all the machines
were mounted with machine guns The
French. during the month, felled nine
German machines and damaged two 9TH
ers in aerial combats. The Germans
claimed to have felled four French
planes.


BY August, 1916. aviation had become
absolutely Indispensable to modern war
fare While year previous fffty-two
machines were needed to drop $50 bombs,
four machines alone could now drop 160
The French dropped more than 1000
bombs during the month on German rail-
way stations. camps. conveys and fac
tories. Aviators by tens and by hundreds
began to win fame flying in all kinds
Of weather, photographing enemy posi-
tions, swooping low over trenches dur
ing attacks to observe infantry progress.
regulating artillery fire, bombarding and
enga aging in air duels. Daily the French
made more than sixty fighting flights
and more than fifty regulation flights
On some days they made two or three
times as many. The central powers
claimed to have fe}led seventy-four enc
my machines. The allies felled ninety
four aeroplanes. disabled sixty-nine
others and brought down ten balloons.

Every comparison that one can make
between the achievement of Haig's army
this year and last demonstrates the enor-
nous improvement that has been made.
Last year the British began at the Somme
with green army; their artillery was but
little trained; they had men, munitions,
machinery, but they did not have ma
chine. When they finished this battle,
which was, in fact, training school, they
had the machine, although they had paid
dearly to assemble it. At the taking Of
Beaumont Hamel last November the Brit
ish demonstrated that they were superior
, in men, guns and aircraft; they had wrest-
ed the superiority from the Germans
hand; he has not regained 1t.


This year the British began where they
left off a year ago. The German had
abandoned his old style of defence. The
Somme had doomed the defence based
upon huge redoubts, deep dugouts and
similar works. The Somme had proved
that these could be destroyed at greater
cost to the defender than to the assailant.
Therefore the German had recourse to a
new system. He held his front by light
works, concreted shell craters, little ma
chine gun shelters; he put few troops in
the front line and counter attacked vigor-
ously when the British advance had slowed
down.


But this method has failed, too. To-day
the British are getting on more rapidly
than they ever did at the Somme. The
elastic" defence has gone the way Of last
years system. The British have got the
Messines- Passchendaele Ridge, as they took
Albert Ridge; they are approaching Rou-
lers, as they approached Bapaume. Only
the weather remains the sure Teutonic
ally; bad last autumn early,'it Is worse
this year even earlier.

FRANCE, Dec. 4.-The best Of many

These men were cut OF in tic Ger

camps they came upon a small body
of British troops which had also been
cut off from their comrades and was
wandering about.


The British Tommies Immediately
charged toward them. The Germans
tried to drive their captives Oft toward
La Vacquerie, but the prisoners hurled
themselves upon their guards and
struggled barehanded until the Tom
mics arrived and disposed of the Ger
mans. The engineers and their COM
rades took the German rifles and
worked their way back with their res
cuers until they were able 10 reach a
point where they could join the British
line.

lorry. which, coming unexpectedly upon
six Germans holding. the crossroads
with machine guns, charged at full
speed, tanklike, bowling over the sur
prised enemy and escaping down the
road before the Germans recovered
from their shock and fright.

army men from the United States who

part of the German counter attacks at
Cambria. Not less than ten American
army medical officers were working in
the British casualty stations along the
Gouzeaucourt front. In fact, they had

began his great offensive.

In April. 1915, the British were prepar-
ing for their subsequent offensive south
ward near La Bassee. The French had
recalled their best troops from this front
to participate in Fochs great Artois oper-
alton. and most OF the few heavy British
guns had likewise gone south. There was
no expectation of any considerable German
operation in the Ypres sector, and Allied
journals were heraldng the coming of the
spring offensive, which was TO throw the
Germans out of France and Belgium. Tow
ard the last of the third week in April an
attack, preceded by the explosion of
mine, had given the British brief hold on
Hill No. so, mound near the point where
the Ypres Confines Canal crossed the
attlefront. Heavy attack and counter
attack on this point occupied the attention
of the world in the next few days.


But on April % came one of the most
dramatic and terrible episodes of the war.
Toward evening the Germans suddenly
loosed vast quantities of chlorine gas
against the French colonial division stand
ing between Langemarck and the fpres-
\ ser Canal at Steenstraete. The result was
a natural and inevitable panic. The black
troops fed south and west toward Ypres
and across the canal. Within brief period

miles between Langemarck and the canal
mere was a gap. The German road to
Ypres was at last open.

dans. When the French troops fled the
Canadian flank was left in the air, while
the troops were themselves exposed TO gas
fumes, and suffered severe losses from this
cause. Yet, despite all the circumstances,
the Canadians hung on. They drew back
their left flank, forming in half circle,
and fought on, holding up for many hours
the onrush of the Germans. Here, on this
front, the Canadian contingent won their
title to rank with the old British army

greatest of the war, the British and
French to-day tore out the entire Ger
man first line and portions of the sec
ond and third over front of more than
twenty miles in Flanders, from Dix
nude, on the north, only ten miles
from the sea, to the Belgian frontier.
just below Warneton, where it is
crossed by the River Lys. In this tre-

Washington, May 16.-Formal an
nouncement that American destroyers
arc in the war zone. operating against
German submarines. was made tonight
by Secretary Daniels after the news
had come from London. The number
and names Of the vessels were not DIS
closed.


Tho Secrctary's statement follows:


"The United States naval vessels
have been operating with the alled
naval forces in European waters since
May 4. A number Of destroyers sailed
from American ports in the latter part
OF April, and all arrived az their des.
tination without accident or delay OF
any kind. hey were ready for opera
tons when they arrived, and went INTO
service Immediately.


"The United States vessels are under
command OF Rear Admiral Sims, who
went TO England and France several
weeks ago TO arrange for active co.
operation between the naval forces of
tho United States and those Of the
other nations at war with Germany.
Plans formulated after reports from
Rear Admiral Sims made as a result OF
his conferences with the British and
French admiraltes are now beng Ell
feetuated.


at has been the purpose Of the
United States navy TO give the largest
measure Of assistance 10 the other
countries 40 war with Germany that is
consistent with the full and complete
protection Of our own coasts and terri
torial waters.


"The Navy Department has received
no reports that engagements have oc-
Cured between the United States yes
sells now in European waters and the
vessels OF the enemy


The disposition Of the destroyers has
been left entirely TO Admiral Sims, who
has worked out a careful plan for use
Of the vessels placed under his COM
mand after conferences both with the
British and French admiralties.


Destroyers have proved the most ef-
icient foe Of submarines. Their value
has been so great that all possible eff
fort has been concentrated by the Navy
Department upon adding to the Ameri-
can fotillas in the shortest time. More
than fifty new boats, swlfter. more pow
erful and seaworthy and more heavily
armed than any now in service. are
being built with all possible haste.
Several will be commissioned early in
the summer.


American destroyers sre sturdy craft,
built for duty at sea, and the conf
dence Of the department in their dura-
bility has been fully justified by the
fact that they arrived on the other
side of the Atlantic ready for imme-
date service. Special attention was
given 10 selecting the crews. Not
man will be sent 10 European waters
who has not had experience and train
ing in destroyer duty. Officials are
confident that the ships and crews VIII
give a good account Of themselves.


Rear Admiral Gleaves. chief Of the
Atlantic fotilla. is busy with vessels
remaining on this side, training add
tional men for service either in Amer
lean or European waters. With great
rush Of recruits to draw upon, all
young. eager men, ready for any danger
in service against the enemy, he is
turning out additional personnel for
the fotilla that promises TO fulfil
American navy traditions for daring
and efficiency.


The department is guarding closely
It's plans for sending other craft than
dsstrovers into the fighting Zones.
There can be no question, however,
that every element of the feet that
can aid in the fight will be used 10 its
utmost.


There does not appear to be any
present necessity for heavy craft IN
addition 10 the British and French
fleets.

To the Editor Of woman's Page:


Dear Madam-wili you please print direo-
tions for knitting a mans sp-on sweater With
round neck and sleeves? A. Z. B.


I am giving you the regular Red Cross
directions for the body of the sweater, with
additional directions for the sleeves. The
regulation Red Cross sweater has no
sleeves.


Use Red Cross needles No. 3 Cast on
eighty stitches. Knit two. purl two
stitches for four inches. Knit plain until
sweater measures twenty-five inches Knit
twenty-eight stitches. bind off twenty four
stitches for neck, loose. Knit twenty-eight
stitches Knit five ridges on each shoulder
cast on twenty-four stitches. Knit plain
for twenty-one inches. Purl two, knit two
stitches for four inches. Sew up sides,
leaving nine inches for armholes. Two rows
single crochet around neck and one row
single crochet around the armholes


For sleeves pick up stitches around the
armholes. dividing them as evenly as pos
sible on four steel needles Knit plain
until the sleeve measures seventeen inches.
Now knit one, knit two together and repeat
this until the sleeve is narrowed down and
ready for cuff. For the cuffs knit two, purl
two until the cuff measures five inches.

lis of the American tank steamer
Vacuum, sunk by German submarine,
and four other survivors who landed
with him on the Scottish coast, suffered
terrible hardships and arc now IN

while two died of exposure in another
boat


Captain Harris said to-day that the

that in less than three minutes the en-
tire complement of the ship, excepting
four men of the engine room staff, who
were either killed by the explosion or

The boats separated and during the

men righted her. but about an hour
later she again turned turtle, and tins
time four men persisted.


II was intensely cold when night fell
and ten Of the fourteen men remain
ing in the boat died from exposure.

was overturned twice IN the darkness.


About noon the next day Captain

boat seven of the nine men survived.

From a staff Correspondent Of The
Associated Press. with the British
Armies in France. May {. Evening -
Infantry attacks and counter attacks
having subsidized for the time being.
there came from the battlefront to-
night only the dull roar OF the never
ending artillery duel


There was stiff lighting all through
last night and early to-day as the Ger
mans threw heavy reserves into coun-
ter attacks. which cost them dearly.
These counter attacks succeeded only
i'm the ncighborhood Of Cherisy. where
the British troops fell back from the
more advanced posts occupied early
yesterday.


Line Like Jigsaw Puzzle


The new British line on the war
maps has the appearance of jigsaw
puzzle, and really reflects the severity
OF the fighting. which has surged back
and forth during the last forty-eight
hours. There are various pockets"
in the front that remain to be cleared
out, and the artillery to-day was pay
ing particular attention TO them. The
guns also make life very unpleasant
for the German inhabitants of Oppy
Wood.


The Canadians resisted all attempts
20 drive them from their newly won
position AZ Fresnoy, and further south
the British troops, which penetrated
another sector of the Hindenburg line.
were holding their gains. New German
units constantly are being identified
among the prisoners taken.


Meantime the German artillery is
making targets Of the villages wreSted
from the Germans in the last two
weeks. Gavrcle. Bailleul. Arleux,
FreSnoy and Monchy are being ground
TO powder by the thousands Of high
explosive shells, in accordance with the
German custom of "strafing" every
place from which they arc driven.


battle-ground Like Picture


The scene of the fight has become
more visible since the British took so
much high ground during the first
rhaSe Of the battle of Arras. It is pos
ciblc now TO look far over the Douai
Plain. From the Vimy Ridge and the
heights about Monchy the war spreads
out below in a great panoramic picture.


The recent activity of the German
artillery lent far more color to the
scene. The entire battle zone seems at
times to be canoped by flying shells.
The barrage curtains set up here and
there appear in the distance like i'm
mense artist palates daubed with
splotchcs Of red, brown, white, black,
gray and pink.


It is possible from the heights to look
upon pretty little French villages far
back Of the shelfre area. and TO see
cities like Douai, Cambria and even
Lille. and one cannot but wonder what
will be their fate as the occupying Ger
mans are broken loose from their near
ly three years grip on this industrially
wealthy section of France.

Sixty-fourth congress, now expired,
enacted number of very important
economic laws, it was notable chiefly
for its response to the popular demand
for national preparedness, inspired by
the European war and the, danger of
conflict with Germany.


Although ample provision has been
made for fortifications, and authority
has been granted by congress to more
han double the standing army of the
country, the metamorphoss of the
United States from a commercial to
4 fighting nation has been wrought
1y the naval increases authorized.
The congress now expired has au-
horized naval arnaments destined to
make Uncle Sam eventually the peer
Of any nation on earth in sea power,
excepting, perhaps, Great Britain.


In the two sessions comprising the
Sixty-fourth congress there have
been authorized and appropriated for
40 less than 11S war craft. Nor is
this all. The first session adopted a
hree-year-building program, the con-
struction of which should be under
taken prior to July 1, 1913. This pro-
gram included this allotment of fight
ing ships: Ten battleships, six battle
cruisers, ten scout cruisers, so torpedo
boat destroyers, nine fleet submarines,
5S coast submarines, one experimental
ubmarine (Neff system), three fuel
ships, one repair ship, one transport,
one hospital ship, two destroyer ten
1ers, one fleet submarine tender, two
ammunition ships, two gunboats.


Naval Vessels Appropriated For.


By the act which adopted this build
ng program congress appropriated
for four battleships, four battle cruis-
ers, four scout cruisers, 20 destroyers,
30 submarines, and one each of these
craft: Experimental submarine, fuel
ship, hospital ship, ammunition ship
and gunboat During the second ses-
sion provision was made for three bat
tleships, one battle cruiser, three scout
cruisers, 10 destroyers, one destroyer
tender, one submarine tender and 1S
submarines.


If the Sixty-fifth congress adopts the
three-year program the remainder of
The units for the reorganized battle
fleet will be appropriated for next
year. Staggering sums have been re-
quired to meet these demands, the ma
val appropriation for the second ses-
sion of the expired congress alone
amounting to almost round half-bil-
lion dollars.


So great have been these eXpendi-
lures that the ordinary sources of rev.
enue are not sufficient and a special
revenue measure had to be passed.
Representative Kitchin, majority lead
er and chairman of the house ways
and means committee, small-navy
man, in drafting the revenue measure
and pressing it to passage through the
house charged full responsibility for
the measure to the advocates of pre-
paredness.


Increase of the Army.


Increases of the regular army and its
congratulations under the national de-
fense act were less striking than the
naval Increases. But the regular army
was increased from an authorized
peace strength of 100000 to an author
lied peace strength of 216,000, capable
of expansion in war time to 256,000.





ness both on land and sea, the consen-
sus of the military experts was that the
United States with its enormous length
of coast line must rely on its fleet to
defend its shores.


In the discussions that preparedness
agitation in congress provoked 1t was
again and again demonstrated that the
temper of the American people Is alb
solutely against big standing army.
Former Secretary Garrison formulated

cabinet.

islanders.

An effort to put the Georgia avenue
line of the Washington Railway and
Electric Company out OF service by
exploding dynamite in the trolley
poles, between Emerson and Farragut
streets, failed early today.


Two poles were shattered, but the
overhead wires were not broken and
the regular morning cars were run
over the line within two hours after
the explosions.


Within half an hour after the ex-
plosion operating officials OF the
company were on the scene, and be-
fore morning traffic was in operation,
temporary repairs were made and no
interruption in the service occurred.
The poles dynamited carried not only
the wires for car operation but cables
and feed wires for the lighting system
as well, according to a statement
Issued by the company.


A dozen Central Office detectives
and policemen are out today to round
up the dynamiters.


Brightwood, Petworth, and Park
View were sleeping soundly when the
two explosions came in rapid success
sion.


Policemen Rush To Scene.


Sergeant Dickson and Patrolman
West were soon at the scene.


They found two poles partly shat
tered, but no serious damage. The
dynamite had been placed In holes
bored in the poles about two feet
from the ground. Below the points
where the dynamite was inserted the
poles were intact


Noticing a long piece Of cord pro-
truding from third pole a few feet
away, the policemen found another
stick Of the explosive, which had not
gone off because the fuse went out
before 1t had burnt UP to the dyna-
mite


Sends Six Detectives.


Sergt. Ned Weldon, in charge of the
detective bureau after midnight, dis
patched six detectives, Burlingame,
Kelly, Embrey, Evans, Warren, and
Joe Grant, to the scene Immediately.


That, the dynamiters went to the
scene and hurried away in an auto
mobile was suggested to the detec-
tives by one resident OF the neighbor-
hood, who said he saw a machine
going out Georgia avenue about the
time the explosion occurred.

Mrs. Edwin A. Skinner. thirty-four
years old. escaped from the Shepherd
and Enoch Pratt Hospital yesterday,
where she had been patient for men
tai trouble: met her two sons, ono
three and the other five years old. as
they came from kindergarten: gave
them poisonous tablets for candy. and
swallowed quantity herself.


The triple poisoning took place in a
public square. The three were found
writhing on the ground by passers-
by and taken to a hospital. Edwin A.
Skinner. jr., the younger, died last
night. and his brother Craig. died an
hour later. Both children were uncon-
scious when found in the square. The
mother was conscious when found, and
stated that she wanted to take her
children with her. She is not expected
to recover.


According to a police investigation,
the woman was brought from the hos
pital Sunday by her husband, who is
employed in Washington, to see her
children. Skinner said she appeared
rational and went back in the evening
willingly. She was missed from the
institution yesterday morning.

mestic science teachers, and the Pilgrim


Mothers were their willing pupils. The

1t is said on good authority that among the

Contrary to accepted tradition, the Indian

The art of conserving all manner Of food by

Food carried when travelling or on the war
path. Venison meat dried, then pulverized, with
dried and finely ground vegetables added prin-
cipally beans and corn, the whole held in mass
by bear grease. Not unlike bologna.

after being liberated by the French and

heaps of debris. Their agricultural I'M
plements and machinery had been

grass seeds trampled.

confiscation of all domestic animals and
poultry in the occupied French provinces
during the last thirty months. caused
many to give way to despair. but joy over
the return of the French eventually DOM
mated all other feelings.

LONDON. July 22.-with redoubled
herceness the battle for the Chemin des
Danes was resumed at dawn to-day and
Is still raging. Wave after wave OF
picked German troops has been hurled
at the dominating French positions on
the ridge. After hand TO hand fighting
the Germans have been repulsed prac-
tically all along the line.


The fiercest struggle ragged on the two
plateaux Of California and Casemate. on
the three miles Of front from Hurtebise
to Craonne, southeast Of Laon. The
Crown Prince was determined to regain
both from the French troops and to
free his army from Its precarious posi-
tion at their foot, right under the French
guns.


At daybreak the first German attacks
were made with large forces led by
picked storming troops. To the west
the Germans were unable to reach the
French trenches, being torn to bits by
the French barrage. To the east the
Germans reached the French trenches,
but were flung back at the point Of the
bayonet.


Again the German troops were sent to
the attack. and French army headquar-
ters reports that they were aided by "a
bombardment Of unheard of intensity"
Great numbers Of German batteries
threw shells on the French trenches
The later attacks were incessant, new
troops being rushed up without interval
to fill the gaps.


On the Casemate plateau the Germans
this time gained a footing. but each
time were sent reeling back down the
slope by the French counter attacks,
leaving their dead piled on the ground.
On the California plateau the French
resistance was equally stubborn, but
during the afternoon the Germans got
into the French FIRST line trenches, where
a hand to hand combat still RACES


On other parts OF the French front
also the fighting has been heavy. At
Verdun the guns were active during the
night ane continued so to-day. Two
German infantry attacks north OF Be-
zonvaux succeeded temporarily. but In
hard fighting they were finally driven
back. Two more attacks on the Meuse
heights were repulsed. In Champagne
also the artillery ire has been very
strong.


The British front has been again the
scene OF very heavy artillery fire, es-
pecially on the front In Belgium. which
continued into the night. Air fighting
and trench raids are also reported.

MANCHESTER, England, Nov. H.
Sir Arthur Yapp, Director of Food
Economy, outlined here to-day his plan
for voluntary food rationing. Follow
ing are the suggested weekly allow
ances Of bread:


Men on heavy industrial or agricult-
ural work, eight pounds; men on ordi-
nary industrial or other manual work,
seven pounds; men unoocupied or on
sedentary work, four pounds eight
ounces.


Women on heavy industrial or agri-
cultural work, five pounds; women on
ordinary industrial work or domestic
service, four pounds; women unoccu-
pied or on sedentary work, three
pounds eight ounces.


Other foods, the allowance Of which
is the same for all, are apportioned as
follows:


Cereals, other than bread, twelve
ounces; meat, two pounds; butter, mar
garine, lard, oils and fats, ten ounces,
and sugar, eight ounces.


Children are not affected by the
scheme, no definite rations having been
fixed for them.

on the question whether Germany or

Senate yesterday by Senator Hitchcock
