day on the war resolution, said England
had first been guilty Of mine strewing,
but the letters, Senator Hitchcock said.
showed Germany to have been first guilty.


Among them was a communication to
the State Department from the German
embassy early in the war declaring that
the American ships Evelyn and Carib,
sunk near the German coast by mines.
had gone down because their captains had
taken aboard Dutch pilots. who did not
know where German mines were planted,
instead of German pilots. An opponent
of the war declaration had argued that
these ships were destroyed by British
mines because Germany would not put
mines SO close to her coast.

acteristic modesty. would not enter until
assured that the President was not about

interest in the big war maps marked

French front, was profound, and their
surprise was dramatic when they saw
maps prepared by the French general
staff showing Verdun in detail.


Have Had Sea War Experience.

ranean between Austrian and French tor
pedo boats at the beginning of the war.

Sir Douglas Haig reports that be-

Both the French and British

dead, while on the British front two

"All information received" says the

ouered from the east in the direction

ception of mile spur of trench that

Arras battlefield.

British continue to move forward. Inc

the great issue. The relentless pressure
- I,Ta af,es

LONDON, Aug. 12.-Stormy weather
last night and to-day prevented the
use of large infantry forces on the
Flanders front, but the artillery bat
tie continues unabated, with the Ger
man batteries particularly busy in the
Ypres sector, where they are shelling
the positions recently lost to the Brit
ish around Westhoek. That the Brit
ism penetrated deeply into the enemy
lines when the Westhoek Ridge was
stcrmed is indicated by to-nights War
Office bulletin, which says that six Ger
man guns were captured, besides 454
prisoners.


The only infantry fighting reported
by General Haig in the last twenty
four hours was sharp combat for a
mine crater at Givenchy, in which the
British won and consolidated the near
lip, and the repulsc of German raid
at Armentieres. Berlin, however, de-
clares that throughout the night the
British were raiding along the whole
of the Ypres salient. while near Holle-
beke, southeast of Ypres, several Brit
ish regiments advanced, only to be
driven back to their trenches with
heavy losses.


British Fliers Out in Force


Despite rain squalls and strong west
erly winds, which naturally favored the
Germans. the British fiers were up in
force yesterday taking photographs and
scouting far behind the enemy lines.
Seven German planes were accounted
for, but five of the Royal Fliers are
missing. two of them having been
forced to descend in hostile territory.


On the day previous, the first IN ten
days when flying was possible from
dawn until dark, the German aviators
attacked in great numbers, losing SIN
teen machines and downing twelve
British planes. II is clear that the
Germans mean to contest TO the last
the British supremacy in the air, whlch ,
was pronounced before the recent OF
fensive. French aviators are now CO.
operating with the Royal Flying Corps
on the Belgian front, and last night
bombed Cortemarck and Lichtenville,
causing extensive fires and violent eX-
plosions in the latter town.


On the Ypres-Menin highroad the
Germans yesterday morning pushed
back the British little in Glencorse
Wood after fierce hand-to-hand en- I
gagement. Haig's men, however, are
low within 1000 yards OF Polygon
Wood. the famous German stronghold,
from which the enemy guns nave I
pounded Ypres into dust during the
last two years.

Berlin reports a livelier lombard /
ment over the whole extent OF the Ar
ras battlefield in Artois, and clear down !
to St. Quentin, with numerous engage
ments. At Fayet, just north OF st. .
Quentin, the French expelled the Ger
mans from the last yard OF the trench
they won there on Thursday. PetaIn's
scouting troops penetrated the enemy
trenches on the western end OF the
Chemin- -des-Dames, returning with prls-
oners, and on the eastern end OF this
highroad not only withstood violent
counter attacks, designed to force them
out of their newly won positions soutn /
of Allies, but made further progress.


II now appears that yesterdays Ger
man ATTACK on NUM- NdlHi''c' ""o M
serious than at first reported, the !
enemy employing strong picked forces,
but gaining nowhere, except on nifty /
yard front. Following their custom ,
after a check in this region, the Ger
man batteries scattered projectiles over
the whole area of Rheims, killing two
civilians and wounding another.


Both Paris and Berlin report that /
the artillery duel north of the Aisne !
and around Verdun is more intense
than usual, indicating large infantry
operations in the near future.

For the past two years reports of
starvation in Germany have circulated
again and again, but always with
prompt denial. These stories came from
travellers, seldom from Germany direct.
Lately there has been a cessation Of
them, and it has seemed that the food
situation within Germany had i'm
proved. Now, however, come statements
by Berlin newspapers to the effect that
the food conditions within the empire
are intolerably bad. The Berliner Tage-
blatt the other day stated that city
jewellers were awaiting the winter with
anxious concern and serious fear; the
foodstuffs prospects were more unfavor-
able than at any time during the war,
and there was danger, in addition
to high prices, which had become ter
rible burden on the masses, that not
even the most absolutely necessary
foodstuffs could be considered as as
sured.


Supplementing this conservative state
ment the Berliner Vorwaerts, in what is
described as plain spoken attack on
the food controller, declares that great
masses Of the German people are not
only hungry, but are literally starving
Condemning the war profiteers and mil
honaires who have boarded food, it
states that the middle class is spending
all it possesses on food, while "forty
millions of the masses are starving and
are unlikely to sit silent" The Vor-
waerts adds these highly significant
words:


eve might have within month an
absolute catastrophe in Germany and a
collapse even worse than the Russian,
resulting in a German defeat and loss
of the war"


It is significant that both the radical
Vorwaerts and the conservative Tage-
blatt express the same opinion, that the
food situation is dangerously critical.
These statements are not travellers
tales or paraphrased reflections from

While little 8-year-old Dorothy Taven-
ner was playing with her dolls in front
of an open crate in her home at 1923
Eighth street northwest yesterday aft
ernoon her dress caught fire.


She ran screaming into the arms of her
mother. who exposed herself to severe
burns in trying to save the life of her
daughter. When the flames were ex-
tinguished the mother carried the uncon-
scious girl into the street and hailed a
passing automobile, in which a hurried
trip was made to George Washington
University Hospital


The clothes of the child had been prac-
dcally burned off, and she was badly
burned from head to foot. The physi-
clans made every effort to save the girl
but failed. She died in two and a half
hours after being admitted.


While the child was in the operating
room the mother screamed in her anguish
and pied to be allowed to see her daugh-
ter. The nurses restrained her and she
was not permitted to see the girl until
she was breathing her last. She rushed
into the operating room and fell fainting
upon the form of her daughter


The little girl was the daughter of Rus
sell and Estelle Tavenner.

Two steamships and ten smaller vessels,
loaded with sugar and glucose. and the

the foot of Congress street. Brooklyn, were
heavily damaged BY fire early today. The
total loss is estimated at $1,000.OO0


Reports that the fire was started by in
cendiary bombs were no, suDstantiated upon
investigation 1t was believed that two ex-
plosions heard about the time the fire was
discovered were caused by the bursting of
ammunition of light defensive guns. Fire
department officials said the blaze originated
through spontaneous combustion.


The damaged steamships are the Baron
Jedburgh' and the Christian Baros. owned
by Furness, Witty & Co.


Sixty members of the crew of the Baron
Judburgh, aroused from sleep by the ex-
plosions and the smoke from the fire, fled
from the ship. They swarmed down the
side of the vessel some of them dropping
into the water and swimming to shore


The fire was discovered by Charles
Lehmke, a watchman. He told the police
that the fire started on the dock, which was
loaded with general merchandise Fire
Chief Heeferman began an investigation as
to the cause of the explosions Immediately


The smaller vessels damaged were all tugs
and lighters.


Owing to the nature of the ships cargoes,
dense smoke, carrying strong. sweet odor,
spread over the waterfront and part of
lower Brooklyn. 1t affected the eyes and
throats of the firemen. who, under difficulty,
worked an hour before they discovered the
main source of the blaze.


Reserves were called out from the four
nearest police precincts and ambulances
were summoned from the Brooklyn. Jew
ish and Long Island hospitals. Captain
Tunney, of Manhattan police headquarters,
detailed twenty detectives to make an in
vestigatiOn.


Except for the Christian Baros all the
craft were virtually destroyed. The Baros
and the Jedburgh came here recently from
the Platte River loaded with manila hemp
and gasoline.

broke out On the 3000-ton Ward liner
Esperanza, which was tied up several

So far there has been in almost, every
German household a sacredly conserved
though slowly disappearing supply Of
delicacies saved from fuller years. or
Transferred" as the Germans put it, in
the days before the food regulations
were too strict. There were honey, mar
malade. canned fruits and vegetables,
preserved meats. condensed milk and
other priceless treasures that made
many unpalatab1e meals eatable. But
pantry shelves are emptier now, and
the opportunities for filling them up
against the winters demands are few.
The two and one-half pounds Of sugar
which were allotted per capita for pre-
serving fruit failed to produce the
necessary results because fruit has been
scarce and the prices almost prohibi:
tive. Last year, too. there were still
fragmentary imports Of foods from
neighboring neutrals. Now these have
practically disappeared. So Mrs. Hub
bard's impoverished and disappointed
canine has lots of human company in
Germany this year.

Maximum prices have been another
stumbling block of the food problem.
Whenever the excessive demand raised
the prices in Germany the various au-
thorities Immediately took advantage
of their power to fix maximum prices,
above which the article could not be
sold. under severe penalties. Invaria-
bly, the result was the same. The article
disappeared from the markets. Scant
supplies reappeared for CUMBERLAND"
traffic at twice or three times the au-
thoritative price. but the bulk of the
supply disappeared completely. Enor-
nous amounts of valuable foodstuffs
are known to have been wasted in this
way. Perishable foods were, often
thrown away by producers who refused
to yield to the maximum price orders.
The authorities prosecuted these relent-
lessly where they could be reached. but
they never cured the evil. Only where
the maximum price fixing was accom-
panied by the government seizure of
the supply and complete government
control. as in the case of grain, potatoes
and meat. could this be counteracted.
The problem will always remain one of
the most interesting phenomena of
these abnormal economic conditions.

Tiflis. Caucasus. April 2O.-The Rus
sian revolution came to the Caucasus
several days after it had won at Pet
rograd. and the new order was put into
effect without hitch and with great
enthusiasm. The new government was
ratified by one of the most picturesque
public gatherings that has been held
anywhere in the Russian Empire.


The peoples Of Tiflis and all neigh
boring districts were invited to at
tend this huge ratification meeting.
For several hours before the hour set
for the meeting the bridge over the
Kura and the streets leading to the as
sembly square were filled with incom-
ing delegates, serious and silent, i'm
pressed with the Importance OF their
mission.


1t was the largest mass meeting OF
Caucasian peoples that has ever been
held. In the great square six plat
forms were raised and the crowd was
simultaneously addressed from all six
platforms, the area being too large to
enable any speakers voice to carry
across the entire crowd.


Every Element Represented


The crowd included every element in
the muti-racial population of this part
Of Russia. There were wild mountain
tribes, Lesgians, Avars, Chechens and
Swanetians in long black cloaks and
sheepskin caps. Their homes lie in the
recesses of the Caucasus range. Sunk
in patriarchal feudalism, many of them
did not know. until the war brought
them in touch with the outside world,
whether they were subjects Of the En-
peror Of Russia or the Sultan of Tur-
key.


Hundreds of the picturesque peas
ants Of the province of Georgia were
also there. The Georgians are politi-
cally the most advanced of all the
races in the Caucasus, having in the
last twenty years developed every form
of Western political thought. Then
there were Armenian merchants, the
Tartar peasants of the East Caucasus,
men from the railway works and the
oil fields at Baku, and the student ele.
ment was prominent.


The platforms were occupied by So
cial-Democratic leaders, who hereto
meetings in secret. They called upon
the people to preserve the public order.
While they were speaking regiment
of the Tifis garrison, headed by their
colonel, marched into the square. eve
have come" said the colonel, "to put
our services unreservedly at the COM
mard of the provisional government.
Long live Great Russja!"


Then a soldier orator took the coll
onel's place on the platform. "Let US
not forget" he said, that over yonder
in Germany we have brothers too
crushed under the same tyranny from
which we have now, thank God, been
delivered. May God grant that the
hour of their deliverance also may
strike soon"


Message from Grand Duke


In an automobile drove up the chief
of staff of the Caucasus army, who
mounted the platform and read mes
sage from Grand Duke Nicholas, in
which the latter stated that he real
lied the old regime had got to go, but
asked the people to preserve quiet and
keep the army free from political
strife.


Among the distinguished guests"
who visited the various platforms were
twenty political prisoners who had
been in the dungeons of Tifis prison
since 1905. when thew were implicated
in local attempt at revolution. There
were women speakers, too, representa-
tives of the Women's League of Post
office Employees and of the Women's
Educational League. There were
speeches in ten different languages, in
'cluding Russian, Georgian, Armenian,
Tartar and six mountain dialects.


A band played the "Marseillaise" at
frequent intervals, the troops present.
ing arms, the peasants doffing their
hats and many voices joining in the
chorus. After four hours the meeting
quietly dispersed.

reunion was arranged, and now

week ago offered the most stubborn

retire without further fighting.


Worn Away Bit By Bit.


The newly occupied ground opens
many possibilities for the British
forces.


Retirement by the Germans from
BapRume, an important strategic
point, is now confidently predicted.
For two years British troops have
pounded increasingly toward this DO
sition. Even winters SHOWS and
frosts have not stilled the method
cal British bombardment on German
positions. Bit by bit Haig's troops

One week ago the British drove for
ward sensationally northwest of lie
Sars and near Petit Miraumont. At that

mans strategic position after this
fresh British advance was such that
retreat was likely. 1t was not ex-

perate effort by the enemy to

ties. Preliminary information, how
ever, discloses that British forces are
now within four miles OF Bapaume.


Butte de Warlencourt, of bloody
memory; Serre, Pys, Miraumont and

hands. All have witnessed some of
the most bloody fighting on the west
ern front.


The other advance by British forces

Turkish forces before they were
into surrender, Is now al

potamian forces. The Turkish gar
rison appears to be trapped in much

AFIELD, April 16.-British troops
fought their way forward in the out
skirts of st. Quentin and Lens today.


Just north of st. Quentin, they took
the village of Troissauvages.


Around three sides of Lens they
were fiercely fighting against German
defenders and slowly encircling the
coal city.


The Germans fought desperately
while in the town itself they strove
frantically to remove guns and sup
plies.


Again early today the Germans
threw two more strong attacks at
British positions at Monchy lie Preux.
Both failed. The British artillery, con-
centrated in a devastating fire,
slaughtered the massed attacking
forces of Teutons.


Another German attack, likewise in
great force, was made on both sides
of the Bapaume-Cambrai road against
Hermies, Noreuil, and Lagnicourt.


The British held firm at Hermies
and Noreuil, but the enemy obtained
a foothold on a spur 200 yards to the
north of Penebaling and Lagnicourt.


Immediately, however, the British
counter-attacked and swept the
enemy out.


The Germans lost heavily in this
attack and the subsequent British
counter attack.

VIENNA February 20, via London.
February 23.-The intense cold weather
has passed and a thaw has set in,
which has solved the fuel difficulty Of
Vienna and incidentally greatly facil-
itated the importation of foodstuffs.
The flour mills, which were shut down
owing to frozen rivers, are again in
operation and full bread rations are
once more in force.


Emperor Charles has been tireless
worker in the campaign to relieve
economic conditions. and tho imperial
teams are still hauling coal for the
populace. The sight of the blooded
stock, heretofore only harnessed to
state coaches, hauling heavy coal
trucks is one Of the curious wartime in
cidents in the Austrian capital. The
emperor recently banished wheat bread
from the officers mess at army head
quarters, and had both wheat bread and
flour removed from a special train
which was taking his brother, Arch
duke Macmillan. to Constantinople. In
issuing this latter order the emperor
remarked that if the common soldiers
the people and himself were contented
with black bread, the party on the train
should be also.

Declines and dragging sales, with
uneven prices. featured the week in
the fruit and vegetables markets. the
Department of Agriculture announced
last night in its weekly review.


The report shows a continued de-
preston in the potato markets, with
prices generally lower in primary and
jobbing centers and movement check
ed by hesitation on the part of buy
ers and sellers.


Virginia continues to be the leading
shipper of sweet potatoes, which have
shown a firmer trend, although the
tone of the markets generally is un-
even.


Barrel apples show a further slight
decline. and a feature of the market
has been its continued dullness and
sagging prices.


Bean prices have shown a down.
ward trend. with demand slow. Re-
stricted tinplate for Gamers is given
as one cause of the slack market.


The onion market has been slow
and dragging. With business light,
the bulk Of the stock has gone into
storage awaiting higher prices.


The celery market continues to hold
up good, with little change. and cab
bage has been fairly steady, though
demand in most Eastern markets has
been light


Grape shipments, excepting from
California, have been light. and pears
have been falling off, although New
York shipped more than last week.


Lettuce continues slight above pre-
vious weeks. with the Eastern and
Southern States shipping normal
amounts, and California leading with
forty-five cars for the week, an in
crease of seventeen over last week.

The series between the Giants and
White Sox for the worlds baseball
championship 10 the fourteenth clash
for supremacy between pennant win
ners Of the National and American
Leagues. A series arranged between
the Boston Americans and the Pitts
burgh Nationals back in 1903 was the
first interleague championship battle,
and the interest in that series did
not give the least idea that within
q few years such contests would make
up the sport classic of the United
States.


There was no friendly rivalry be-
tween the two major leagues when
that first series was played, The
American League had forced recoz-
milton from the older organization but
short time before John /. Taylor
hurled his challenge at Barney Drey-
fuss for q championship series. Tay-
lor's Boston club, managed by Jimmy
Collins. had won the American League
pennant. and Dreyfuss' Pittsburgh
club. with Fred Clarke at the head,
had been victorious in the National
League. But many of the National
Leaguers still refused to admit that
Ban Johnson's organization was of
major league Laliber, and although
the leagues apparently were at peace,
the feeling that prevailed was any thing
but friendly. However, Dreyfuss ac-
cepted the challenge. He was a loser.
but he had paved the way to the
big event which world series have
since become.


Then came a year without a series
-fhn nptx /.
the present time. In 1904 Jimmy Collins
again lead his Boston team home in
first place and John McGraw won his
pennant as leader OF the Giants. Nat
urally the talk OF another series
sprang up. and the Boston club was
anxious to defend its title of worlds
champions. After much deliberation
an announcement was made that the
New York club would not play such
a series The late John T. Brush
was then the directing spirit of the
Giants. and he had not entirely for
gotten the wounds inflicted by the
American League during the base
ball war. That fall the National Com
mission passed rule making such
q series between the major league
pennant winners obligatory. and there
has been no break since the 1904 sea-
son.


OF the games played to date the
American League has the edge on
the older organization. OF the thir-
teen series between these organfza-
tions the representatives OF Ban
Johnson's league have been victori-
Gus eight times and the National
League representatives have been
victorious five times. The Ameri-
can League has won thirty-eight
games, against thirty-four for the
senior organization, and two games
have ended with the score tied. In
the early days the honors usually
went to the National League, four of
the first six series going against the
johnson clubs. In 1910 the tide turn
ed, and since that year the younger
league has been q rather consistent
winner. The victory of the Braves
over the Athletics In 1914 is the only
break in a string Of American League
successes since 1910. Six of the past
seven series have resulted in VIC
tories for the American League.

With each fresh attack along this
front it becomes palmer that both
sides are equipped with enough artil-
lery to smash the first lines 10 pieces
and penetrate for at least half a mile
at almost any point and at almost any
time selected. This, however, Will not
win the war. The question Will be
which can maintain the same success
on long continued operations, or which
can invent the process which will actu-
ally pierce the others defences on
front broad enough for safety and deep

Which can do this, if either. remains
to be seen The Germans were stopped
finally and completely before Verdun,
and the British and French were never
completely stopped on the Somme. But
this is another year, and the Teuton
attacks now show that Germany has
accumulated a vast store OF smmunl-
ton and is ready to exchange shells

even basis than she could last fall,

Poor Russia, torn and rent in
twain, has reached an evil pass
though she has statesmen safe
and sane, they cannot put up
grass; for every time one tries a
trick to bring the bacon home,
some angry voter throws a brick,
and there's a busted dome. And
far off, where the norther piles in
long white drifts the snow, the
ex-czar through his whiskers
smiles, and says, Il told you So"
The exiled monarch's safely
canned, beneath an arctic sky; he
thinks about his native land, and
winks the other eye. Alas, poor
Russia in distress! Her troubles
never stop; she changes so no
sport can guess which bunch will
be on top. One day this party
cuts some ice, the next it's in the
soup; today it's peace at any price,
anon for war they whoop. And
Nicholas, amid. the snow, is swat
ting arctic flies; he's resting while
his whiskers grow, and looking
pretty wise. He sweeps the ice
and sleet away from off his kitch-
en- floor, and digs some paths, so
feet may stray from we'll to hen
house door. The bleak north wind
is blowing strong, and there are
signs of snow, and as the ex-czar
tolls along he sighs, 81 told you
So" WALT MASON.

That is Germany's condition to-day.
She has lost her artillery-sight because
she cannot keep up in the air; she has
lost the initiative in battle, because the
Allies on the Western front can attack
when and where they please. But she
has not lost position yet; she still has
lines Of defence, and she still has men
for defence. No matter how much
ground is taken, Germany cannot be
thoroughly beaten until her reserves of
men are exhausted. And so long as
she has positions to fall back on she
can save her men.


Two other "show places" on the
Western front teach the same lesson
to America. Arras is the scene of a
great battle, dating from April Q. That
battle was still going on when | was
on the ground, and you could feel the
reason with every yard of road you
travelled beyond the city of Arras it.
self. Your motor car tumbled into
gullies and bumped over wooden
trestles which covered mine craters;
you saw German railways torn up and
engines blasted into meaningless wreck
age; trees had been felled and thrown
across the roads.


As the Germans retreated over this
ground they laid mines with perfect
regularity along the roads, and after
they had gone far enough behind they
dropped shells with absolute accuracy
between the hollows which the mines
had made. Roads ceased to exist and
had to be constructed through new
country-and when you are bringing
up thousands Of motor trucks q day
you want more than a dirt road. You
need a metalled road, and you need
it hardened and baked in with the rain
and the sun. While you are making
the roads the Germans, who have still
untouched roads behind them, are forti-
flying their new positions and Smelling
the outposts of the British advance.


So there is another thing which
America can and must do; she can put
at the disposal of all the Allies every
last thing she knows about road
making. She can bring over her own
equipment and send over her own men.
Every mile of road laid down saves
lives for us and sends the Boche hurry
ing faster and faster eastward, and the
faster he goes the less chance he has
to destroy what stands in his way.


If the British had been able to
handle the problem of roads and rail-
ways so per cent faster than they did
after the battle of Arras the linden
burg line could never have held at
Bullecourt and Oppy. The sixty-day
battle for Bully" as the Canadians
call it, with its countless casualties
and its check to the whole eastward
operations, would have been avoided

Great excitement followed the ex-
plosion. A heavy pail of smoke dark
ened the entire town, which has a
population of about 5000. This was soon
lightened by the flames from the burn
ing building. RESCUE squads composed
of other employees at the plant were
quickly formed and a call for assistance
was sent to Philadelphia, Chester, Will
mington and other nearby points The
entire Chester fire department respond
ded. and ambulances from Philadelphia
and Chester were soon at the scene. A
strong guard of Pennsylvania militia
men and cadets from the Pennsylvania
Military Academy was thrown around
the plant and every one except those
assisting in the rescue work were for
bidden to approach.


Fifteen minutes after the explosion
the bodies of the dead and injured were
being carried out They were placed in
any conveyance that happened to be at
hand. Some were taken to the morgue
and hospitals in grocer's wagons and
butcher carts. while others Were placed
in motor cars. Several bodies were
fished out of the marshes 200 yards
from the ill-fated building. and it is
feared that others may have been blown
into the river. still farther away. All
were badly mutilated and many were
burned beyond recognition.

American-owned. though of British reg
istry, has arrived here from London,

with U-boat on the Cornish coast. For
twenty minutes the tanker exchanged
shots with the Submarine. One OF her
men was killed and three others injured

sent the German U-boat to the bottom.

news Of the submarines sinking. in ac-
cordance with the usual practice. The
battle occurred in February, while the
Sequoya was en- route to England from
an American port. The tanker still bears
marks Of the fight and will stay in port
here until repairs are made.


Gave No Warning.


The submarine appeared about dav-
light on the Cornish coast and gave us
no warming until a shot'had smashed the
bridge" said Chief oficer Weeks. The
U-boat was less than a mile away, and
Capt. James at once ordered her fire
returned. Before our gunners could do
so. another shell hit US. Then our men
fired twice but missed the submarine.


"A third shot hit US, killing one of our
men and scattering shrapnel over the
deck. Three received injuries Two more
shots were fired by the submarine before
our gunners' aim told. With his fifth
shot he struck squarely. An explosion
tore a great hole in the U-boat and she
turned over and sank, We cruised
around but were unable to find any sur
vivors''


The Sequoya was loaded with benzine.
Had a shot struck one of the tanks, the
ship probably would have been blown to
pieces.

shattered bridge, wheel house, and life
boat, which have been repaired temper
arily.

The potato season of 1899 was disas-
trous for the planters Of the two lower
counties of the peninsula. Many of them
did not get enough for their crops to pay
for the fertilizer. hauling, labor and
freight. Consequently there was deter
mination among many of them never to
grow another tuber.


But when these planters began to cast
about for some crop to take the place of
potatoes they awoke to the fact that
their lands were better adapted to grow
ing roots than anything else. Some of
the more discerning among them, after
looking over the situation. came to the
conclusion that the fault was in the man
ner of disposal of the crops.


A careful study convinced them that
the reason potatoes were bringing
such meager returns was that they
were not shipped to the right markets,
and not that all the markets in the
country were glutted. The latter fact
was apparent because, despite the low
prices. not enough potatoes were be-
ing raised in the United States to meet
the supply and some tubers were being
imported.


Meetings of the farmers were called
and plan was presented to them. The
result was the organization of the ex-
change. 1t began its work in the
spring of 1900 and Immediately much
sitter market became apparent.

BROWNSVILLE. Tex, March 27.-Two
escaped members of the interned crews
of two German auxiliary cruisers at the
Philadelphia navy yard crossed the Rio
Grande two miles below Brownsville, Sun
day and are now in Matamoros Mexico
opposite here, according to information
received at military headquarters at Fort
Brown. American military authorities
have taken up the matter with Mexican
officials in Matamoros.


Fourteen members of the crews of the
German commerce raiders Kronprinz Will
helm and PrinZ Eitel Friedrich, interned
at the Philadelphia navy yard. made a
dash for liberty last week. All but two
of them were captured inside of the yard
within short time. and officials of the
Navy Department announced their belief
that these two had been drowned in at
tempting to swim the back channel


Despite this announcement. however
Philadelphia authorities expressed the
belief that the two men, Lieut. Chorth
and Hermann Schroeder, machinist mate,
had escaped.

Down from the Alps with flame and sword
There comes devastating horde


Upon Venctia's plain.
With torches snatched from Louyain's


pyre


The Hun proclaims his fierce desire,


And Venice writhes in pain.
Bride Of the Sea. respondent, fair,
Standing in marbled beauty there,


She rues her shameful fate,
Nor hopes to move by beauty's plea
The band that Scared her spouse, the


Sea,


With murder, stealth and hate.
Before the onslaught of the Hun
Old landmarks crumble, one by one,


Where helpless breasts are barred
The treasured tokens of mans art,
Or holy affairs of his heart


Naught beautiful is spared.
Must genius truckle thus to might?
Must beauty vanish from mans sight!


Does Earth move backward then?
Not while the planets move to laws,
Not while there lives primal Cause;


No! Not while faith breeds men!
When Winter rushes from his lair
His ruthless blasts may rend and tear
The blossom on the hill;
But that same stalk shall breast the snow
Till Summer suns again shall show


That God loves beauty still.
The Hun may kill, the Hun may rend,
His little space of power will end;
The world will pass him by.
And from the ashes whence he flies
New hopes, new monuments shall rise
Where Faith shall see through Valor's


eyes


That beauty cannot die.

text:
Special Correspondence of The Star.


NEW YORK February 1.-THE older
woman may regret the fact that the dot
and the block will cover the surface of
many fabrics that she wishes to wear
this spring, hut the Juvenile will not
indulge in any such feeling.


Just why children like polka dots and
checkerboards on their clothes is not
for the fashion writer to tell; let the
Montessoris of the world work that out.
The only fact worth recording is that
Juveniles are far happier when there is
some color thrown over the surface OF
their clothing than when it is quite
plain and uninviting.


Polka dots have belonged to children
for decades. There are few Of us who
cannot. remember that first fine, care,
less rapture" with which we greeted
the polka dot gown that was our first
essay into real clothes.


Whenever one thinks of polka dots
and children one is tempted to recall
again and again Peter Newells delight
full little picture of the child in her
first polka dot gown and the boy with
the mouthorgan, with the little verse
asking if he played a lively tune would
all the polka dots come out and dance:


The very appeal which this bit Of
gayety made in America and the uni
versal human experience that this ia
Their of several children recorded
through his gifted pencil substantiates
the instant connection between child
and a polka dot gown.


Peter Newell once said, when asked
where he got his inspiration for his
merry and insidious cartoons of child
life, that his own children supplied him
with it His boys brought him these
quaint little Jokes, consciously or I'M
consciously. through their actions and
their verbal give and take in the house.


This explanation of his work has al
ways stuck in the memory of the re-
porter who interviewed him, because 1t
gave the clue to the success of his
drawings

PARIS, Aug. 25.-The outstanding
feature Of the battle OF Verdun. in
which the French successfully attained
capture yesterday of IIill 3o4. was the
tremendous use OF gas shells by the
Germans.


Gas shells have been employed princi-
pally. heretofore, in preparing the way
for an infantry assault and In breaking
up counter attacks. In the present
battle the Crown Prince. preparing to
defend his army from the attack which
he knew was coming. decided to use
gas extensively in shelling the French
big gun batteries during the terrific
cannonade which preceded the advance.
his object being to deluge the French
gunners with poisonous fumes and
thus silence the batteries and enable the
Germans to hold the trenches which
were being bombarded.


The French artillerymen. by wearing
gas masks all the time. were able to
work the guns without cessation. COM
pletely pulverizing the enemy positions.
The Germans rained a storm of gas
shells upon the woods back of the
FTcNCH lines tIlIouSH WHICH tHe pollus
had TO pass to reach their own first line
trenches before beginning the attack.
and also filled the woods between the
lines with poisonous fumes. 1t was
asphyx!ation into which Petain's men
dashed. much like the cloud of black
smoke which the inhabitants Of Mars
used in H. G. Wells's story of the war
of the worlds.


French troopers who were overcome
and removed TO hospitals were found to
be badly burned about the body while
the face. protected by the mask. was
unharmed. The effect of the fumes was
corrosive eating through the clothing.
The gases used were heavier than those

phuric acid fumes when they came in
contact with moisture. Arsenic and
phosphorus appear to have replaced

Dear Madam-Win you kindly print the dl-

With amber needles. cast on fifty-four

steel needles, having thirty-six stitches on

NORTHERN ITALY. Dec 6.-Lieuten-
ant Ancillotto Of the Aviation Corps
has executed one of the most daring
exploits Of the war, telescoping an Aus
trian balloon which was observing
Venice from the Piavc line. passing
through the gas bag with parts of the
envelope about his propeller and win
ming a government bonus OF 5000 lire
for his exploit.


Enemy drachens, or observation bal
looms, have been numerous and trouble
some all along the line, and the authori-
ties have offered 1000 lire for every
ono destroyed. Ancillotto had brought
down two within the last few days and
Yesterday went after his third. He
rose from Maestro, suburb of Venice,
in an S0-horsepower machine and
ascended high above the drachen. Then
he began a series Of glides close above
the balloon to drop incendiary bombs
as he passed.


On one of his glides the aviator mis-
calculated. and instead of passing over
the Drachen struck it squarely amid
ships. There was terrific rip and
tear as the airpane shot through the
envelope and emerged with its tatters
On his propeller. The great volume of
gas released took fire from the engine
Of the airplane, and the Drachen was
burned in midair, together with it's oc-
cupant.


Lieutenant Ancillotto was scorched,
but uninjured He guided his machine
back to.thc aviation field, where he was
received with rapture. His gray car
was burned black as charcoal, but
otherwise il was uninjured.

The most terrific bombardment Germany
has yet concentrated against the French
lines was massed Saturday night in a des-

Today. with the consultations Of the

pagne five or six miles from the front II
seemed as though this fire was solely to
vent German rage at the French success.
The shells fell in many villages where Red
Cross ambulances were stationed including
8. section OF the American ambulance corps
waiting to go to the front for wounded.
All the Americans escaped unharmed.


The Champagne struggle began early in
the week with extensive preparations for at
tack by the Germans The French defend
ers were fully apprised Of these prelimi.
nares. They saw construction Of new
trench from which the German attack was
destined 10 start They knew that three
new divisions Approximately $4,000 men),
including the Seventy fourth Hanover Regi-
ment, had been brought up into line. The
Hanoverians were to bear the brunt of the
assault. lneN Knew lUeSe ATTACKING troops
had been rehearsed back of the line for the
part they were to play in the struggle.


Then the French egan preparations of
their own for an attack For three days
the French artillery roared out prepara-
tory fire. Late Saturday evening this
preparation decreased. The French pur-
posely timed the slackenng fire to deceive
the Germans into thinking an attack was
imminent. But the usual attacking hours
passed Along toward 1880 the Germans
began to figure that there was no assault
coming. The enemy hauled down their OBJ.
servation sausage balloons, apparently con-
WINGED that the day ending in tran

Suddenly, at 7:45, the French reopened
n redoubled artillery bomhardment Al
most simultaneously the French infantry
leaned out of their trenches.


Across the line the Germans tried hastily
to shoot up their observation "sausages'
in an endeavor to find out what was hap
pening. But before the balloons could
reach heights sufficient for observation the
French had won their victory. Ioilus held
the tops of both Monts Teton and Haut--
exactly the objectves planned for them.


Within less than five minutes the Ger
mans, with the gigantic artillery concentra-
tion which they had massed for their abor-
tive attack opened the most terrible bonn
hardment | have yet witnessed anywhere
along the French front. The SUBMITS of





oped in seething smoke. The sides We're a
living furnace Of burning grenades. inCend-
airy shells exploding munitions caches and
flaming materials generally.


Into this literal furnace the Germans
launched their counter-attacks. The desper-
ate character of the fighting which ensued
was apparent from the countless rockets
that famed into the skies. French and
German troops both sent them up, signaling
advances and retreats, calls for lengthening
or shortening of the barrage fire, a change
in artillery ranges and other fluctuations
Of the battle. Night fell on this scene.

was as light as day.


The Germans finally gave il up, They

Before morning the pous had concentrated

Honeymoons have been the fashion
so long their origin seems enshrouded
in the mists of antiquity.


Just who ever started the first hon
eymoon is not known, but its incep-
ton was without doubt happy one.


June being the accepted month for
weddings, naturally 1t is the time when
most honeymoons are taken.


1t is the grand climax of the we'd
dings. The bride has been looking for
ward to it for months, maybe for
years.


After the ceremony (under which
the poor little bride has almost brok-
en- down through the nervous strain
and the bridegroom has felt about as
lively and important as the only male
in the audience of a national suffra-
gette meeting) after the congratula-
tory expressions from friends and rel
atives; after the wedding supper; af-
ter the rice and old shoes have been
thrown-comes the wedding trip.


On the train comes the pretense of
fooling conductor, passengers and por-
ter; that they are really not newly
married couple must be assumed.


That stunt has been pulled by every
body who ever got married and yet no.
body ever got away with it.


Anybody can spot bride and bride
groom anywhere and any time.


They show it as plainly as If they
wore tag upon which in large letters
was printed the words. 1--WE Are New
ly Married-Have a Heart"


Honeymoons are the happiest times
of the married state. Can't you look
back across the years and see yourself
when you had the heavy role in that
little drama of your life? Can't you
see again the sweet little star who
played opposite you, so timidly, so
trustingly, as she kept one eye on her
suitcase and the other on your pocket
book?


All, Time, you are a heartless old
thief. You steal away our years of
dew-kissed happiness; you rub out the
rose bloom of youth and you rub in the
wrinkles, but you can't reach the hu-
man heart, you old crook-thank God
you can't touch that, or you would age
that too.


The heart may remain young for
ever, for we are only as old as we feel.


All you can do is whiten the hair and
rumple the skin, bend the back and
make slow the step, but when couple
love each other, their hearts often turn
back to the honeymoon days and it
helps brighten the journey the rest of
the way.


Here's to the honeymoon-may it
never wane.-Florida Times-Union.

BRITISH ARMY HEADQO AKI Eho
IN FRANCE, Nov. 22.-The impression
which existed in the minds of many
soldiers that the British tanks were
freaks of little value as instruments
of war is being wiped out on account
of the achievements Of the great army
of these mighty engines which on
Tuesday morning broke through the
rain Hindenburg line and carried the
war miles into enemy territory.


The work which the tanks did on
that first day and have been doing
ever since is one Of the most striking
features Of the war. Infantry, artil-
lery and cavalry all played their part,
but the tanks drove the entering
wedge without which this triumph
probably would have been impossible.


In few hours they tore to shreds
lines Of barbed wire the demolition Of
which by a concentration of artillery
would have required many days. Fur
thermore, their employment made pos
sible the arrangement Of the secret
attack, which would have been out OF
the question had the artillery been
brought into play.


The tanks have demonstrated fully
their power in saving the lives OF men
and in conserving ammunition. he
casualties among the infantry which
followed the tanks into action were
exceedingly light. Two battalions, for
instance. had only one casualty each.
and another suffered the loss Of only
three men.


Few Casualties Among Tank Crews


The casualties among the crews OF
the tanks also were very light on the
opening day, which is the only one for
which reports have thus far been re-
ceived. There were several hundred
tanks. and out of all the men who went
forward in them il appears that less
than twenty were killed and less than
one hundred wounded. Many Of these
casualties were due to the fact that
men left the tanks to perform some
work in the open, where they came
under the fire of snipers.


The performance of the tanks was
the more remarkable because there
was only a short time to prepare for
their use. Some of the tanks were
veterans, but many had never been IN
an engagement before, and the crews
lacked actual fighting experience.
Moreover, il was necessary to train the
infantry to cooperate with them. All
this was accomplished in a very few
weeks.


In addition. a great amount Of work
was done to get the tanks into posi-
ton and bring forward their fuel.
Many hundred tons Of petrol were
brought Up secretly and stored pend
ing the attack. II was done so quietly
that few soldiers in the territory in
volved knew what was proceeding.


The advance of the tanks, with their
general leading the way in the mont
tor Aging his flag, was the most i'm
pressve sight imaginable. For miles
they were lined up along the British
front. and when they started forward
it was like great ceremonial parade.
Back OF them came the infantry, giving
the final touch TO the picture.


Tanks have been engaged in some
bitter fighting since they entered
enemy territory. They crushed their
way through barbed wire easily, tear
ing great gaps for the infantry, and
il was not until they had made con-
siderable advance that strong resist
ance was encountered.


Tanks Charge Big Guns


The stiffest fighting was at Lateau
Wood, south of Masnieres. There the
tanks engaged a number Of German
field and heavy guns and won the day
against them. One tank deliberately
charged a 5.9-inch gun and cleaned out
its crew with its machine guns.


Cantsing fell before one tank which
never had seen action until that time.
II charged into the village, making it
untenable by the vigorous action Of it's
guns. Twelve tanks lod the way into
Marcoing. Their crews previously had
studied maps and been assigned posts,
and the tanks went about the bushes.
methodically, each one taking up the
position designated. These twelve NOV
able forts completely dominated the
place.


At Ribecourt the tanks arrived just
as the Germans were sitting down to
breakfast The crews of the tanks got
their morning meal from the food pre-
pared for the enemy.

tanks assisted in taking. They have
been swarming over the whole great
territory annexed by the British, and

is told it will make remarkable his
tory

ounce Of their strength into an at
tempt TO stem the rising tide.

PARIS, Jan. 21.-The French Govern
ment paid tribute this afternoon to the
Americans who have fallen fighting for

of Alan Seeser. A sort of MEMORIAL
ceremony was held in Frances foremost
theatre, the Comede Francaise.


Nine. SECOND Weber, the tragedienne,
recited some of the poems of Alan
Seeger from the stage. She wore Greek
white classical garb and falling from
her head and flowing behind was an
American flag. AS she finished the reci-
taton she seized the flag and flung out
her arm in a fine gesture, unfolding the
Stars and Stripes. There was great en-
thusiasm in the crowded theatre.

meth Weeks. The sacrifice of the Ameri-

skv's mind Yesterday when her sus-

decided TO follow him. Ostransky left
his home at 1863 East Broadway and

With her fve-year-old daughter,

Cohen apartment. She found her hus-
band in the kitchen. Mrs. Cohen was
making him some coffee. Wife and
daughter united in a plea for Ostran-
sky to return to his family. Finally
il was Mrs. Cohen who told him to go.

both bullets entering Mrs. Ostransky's

minute later. Ostransky had fired the
two remaining bullets into his temple,
but was conscious. He said that the
shooting of his wife was accidental
and that he was glad Mrs. Cohen was
dead.


"'She spoiled my married life" he
said.


Mrs. Ostransky said her husband, who
is clothing manufacturer, had been
infatuated with the woman for FIVE
years.


Ostransky was taken to Gouverneur
Hospital, charged with homicide.
There is little chance of his recovery.
